utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Prosecutor, you completed your submission, did you not? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now we hear from Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The defendant, General Blaskic, has only one position with respect to the subject of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me one minute. I do not see the transcript. (Pause) Mr Hayman, you may proceed. Presentation by MR HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The accused has only one position with respect to the subject of whether this Tribunal has the power to issue subpoenas to nation states and that is as follows. Whatever powers and processes to which the prosecution has access in that regard, the accused must have equal access. I believe there is no disagreement on this issue between the Prosecutor and the defence. Indeed, it is hard to imagine how anyone could disagree in light of the requirements of Article 21 as well as broader notions of international law, fairness and protection of an accused's rights. That being our position, the court -- the Tribunal may be wondering: why did the defence wish to participate in these proceedings from the earliest appointed time? In fact, why would we want to be here at all, given the length of this hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Hayman. When you say "earliest point in time", you submitted a subpoena to Judge Jorda on what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We filed a request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I know it was after I had signed the subpoenas, addressed to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So it was much later, your Honour. It was on February 28th. When I say "earliest point in time", I am referring to the application of the Prosecutor for issuance of a subpoena duces tecum on January 10th, 1997. That is an application that was filed ex parte with no notice -- first of all, no service on the defence and no notice of an ex parte filing; in other words, no notice of the bare fact that ex parte contact with the Tribunal occurred, which I would submit is normal and appropriate, so at least the defence can raise the issue: is it something to which we should have notice and should have a right to participate? So when I say "from the earliest point in time", I am referring to January 10th 1997. If not then, then certainly at the moment at which the proceedings became public. My understanding is as of January 10, 1997 the proceedings were in camera and they were closed proceedings. I do not know that for a fact. I have not been given transcripts of those proceedings by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The subpoena was submitted to me as the confirming judge and I have no relationship to the matter, the trial; that is being handled by Judge Jorda. You submitted your subpoena to Judge Jorda. Judge Jorda then transferred the matter to me. I do not have the record, but it was at a later date. Finding that he did not wish to handle the subpoena for you, because it would require ex parte involvement with you, considering that the prosecution should not be involved in those deliberations. Therefore he transferred it to me, but the initial subpoena that I signed, I signed because I confirmed the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, your Honour, I understand that view. Our position, though, is the initial subpoena matter was not referred to your Honour by Trial Chamber I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What initial subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The application from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Of course not, because I was the confirming judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Nor do we believe there is any express provision in the Rules or the Tribunal Statute that provides on the eve of trial for the Prosecutor to go to any Trial Chamber other than the Trial Chamber. I do not know to which Trial Chamber the Prosecutor should have gone. I know the Prosecutor did not consult with Trial Chamber I before coming to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How have you been prejudiced?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We believe we have been prejudiced because we have been excluded from the proceedings until todays date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How have you been prejudiced?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have been prejudiced, your Honour, because the Prosecution has obtained the issuance of two subpoenas to two nation states. They have obtained documents pursuant to at least one of those subpoenas. They have had unequal access to the subpoena power. The defendant has not been able to obtain issuance of any subpoenas on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Because you did not submit one until a certain point in time and now that request for the issuance of a subpoena has been suspended pending the resolution of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had the proceedings not been in secret, your Honour, we would have filed our application on January 17th 1997 and would have requested one subpoena issued from the Tribunal, seeking both the inculpatory documents that the Prosecutor apparently seeks as well as the exculpatory documents that the Defence seeks. We think that would have been a far better, far more even-handed procedure that would have protected the accused's rights under Article 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What rights would he have?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He has rights to equal access to whatever subpoena powers this Tribunal has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Exactly. You have submitted the subpoena now to Judge Jan. It has been received to this Trial Chamber and you have been notified that Judge Jan will meet with you ex parte, that is without the presence of the Prosecutor, to consider that subpoena. That will happen as soon as we conclude these hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the eve of trial there is limited time. There is limited time to pursue leads, to conduct follow-up investigation. I do not know what documents the prosecution has already obtained pursuant to the subpoenas issued by your Honour. I do know that we have obtained none of the exculpatory documents we seek. I do not know when or if we will ever get them or if we do get them, there will be sufficient time to utilise them properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecutor will have no access to your request for a subpoena, nor will the Prosecutor be present when that subpoena is considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I served my request on the Prosecutor, your Honour. I did not seek ex parte contact with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you wish to serve it on the Prosecutor, you may, but it will be considered by Judge Jan when we finish these proceedings without the presence of a Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not raise that issue. I believe the Prosecutor has sought for tactical reasons to obtain its subpoenas from your Honour in secret, without notice even of an ex parte contact to the defence, and they have thereby gained a tactical advantage in violation of Article 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then you need to say that, but take a look at the rule that allowed the Prosecutor to come to me, and that is rule ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: 54, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Actually it is Article 19 that I am referring to, I believe. Yes. Article 19 provides: "Upon confirmation of an indictment the judge may, at the request of the Prosecutor, issue such orders and warrants for the arrest, detention, surrender or transfer of persons or any other orders as may be required for the conduct of the trial." I was proceeding under Article 19 because I am a confirming judge. Believe me, I do not look for additional work. I have enough to do. The subpoena came to me pursuant to Article 19.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can say this, your Honour. Trial Chamber 1 expressed some amount of surprise and enquired of Mr Harmon why he came to this Trial Chamber on the eve of a trial that is before trial Chamber 1. I think we would all agree at some point in time the baton passes to the Trial Chamber that will conduct the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And that Trial Chamber, Judge Jorda's Trial Chamber, Trial Chamber 1, referred the matter to me. I attempted to refer it to that Trial Chamber, as you know, at that hearing that was conducted. It was his decision that he did not want to handle it. He wanted me to handle it. Then when you filed your subpoena, I attempted to refer that to him, because I considered that he should look at it to see whether or not there is at least a facial claim of relevance and materiality to the issues that will be raised at trial. I am not in the best position. He again made the determination that it should be handled by this Trial Chamber and it will be handled by Judge Jan ex parte without the presence of the Prosecutor when we conclude these hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, your Honour. I understand based on the hearing before Trial Chamber 1 it refers my application for a subpoena to this Trial Chamber because of the fear of an inconsistent ruling had it retained that matter, because this Trial Chamber had already ruled on the Prosecutor's application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is one of the considerations that was in the Trial Chamber's determination -- I was not present at the hearing -- but the other reason was once again I had handled it pursuant to Article 19.2. If you are suggesting that there was any impropriety, then you need to raise that with Judge Jorda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am suggesting, your Honour, that the Prosecution sought to proceed ex parte and before this Trial Chamber in the manner that they did in order to obtain a tactical advantage which they have gained as a result of proceeding in that matter. I am not faulting this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The tactical advantage they gained, if any, was that they submitted a subpoena before you did, and, of course, it may not have occurred to you that the Tribunal would be issuing subpoenas, but when you found that a subpoena had been issued and rightfully so, you are now attempting to proceed the same way and we welcome that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I discussed this question with the Office of the Prosecutor last fall, your Honour, about whether the Tribunal had subpoena powers. I was told at that time they did not know. This was in casual conversation. I do not think they should be held to those representations but at the first moment we learned that the Prosecutor believed there was such a power, we began preparing our own application. I am simply saying for a period of roughly 45 or 60 days they conducted themselves in secret to gain a timing and a tactical advantage over the defence, which they have gained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And you understand that the whole confirmation process envisioned by Article 19.2 and rule 47 of our rules is an ex parte proceeding, that is the Prosecutor comes to the confirming judge for confirmation. The judge looks at the materials and then makes a determination as to whether a prima facie case has been established. The continuing relationship with the confirming judge flows from that same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You understand that the confirmation of the indictment process is ex parte, your Honour. I do take issue with continuing ex parte contacts in the nature of trial preparation such as clearly these subpoenas are in the nature of trial preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am not going to argue back and forth with you. You will have your opportunity either this evening or tomorrow to meet with Judge Jan ex parte in private to discuss the subpoena that you have submitted. The reason is the subpoena that you submitted to Trial Chamber 1 that was included in your motion for a request for a subpoena is very different from the one that you then submitted to this Chamber. That matter needs to be resolved. You have asked for, I think, three or four different requests, and in the motion that you filed you only supported your claim for the documents with respect to -- I think it was item number 10. So there are some matters that need to be resolved ex parte in camera with the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am not seeking to take up the merits of that application, your Honour. I am simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is one thing. I do not understand your allegation that the prosecution has gained tactical advantage. Any document that the prosecution obtains consequent upon the subpoena issued and that the prosecution wants used in evidence will be given -- a copy of that will be provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is not correct, your Honour. We have not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think under the rules all documents, all evidence that is to be adduced against the accused has to be given to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have not triggered the reciprocal discovery rules in our case. We have not received all such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not talking about the discovery rules. If you think you do not have sufficient time and the subpoena was submitted late, you can satisfy the Trial Chamber to grant you time. I do not understand what tactical advantage the prosecution can take. You can always satisfy the Chamber that: "The subpoena was submitted very late. We have not been able to prepare ourselves". I am sure if your request is reasonable according to the Chamber, it will grant you time. I do not know what technical advantage you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to address both of your comments, your Honour. First, with respect to Rule 66, we had not triggered the reciprocal discovery provisions of Rule 66. So we are not receiving and have not received copies of all documents that the prosecution intends to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is your choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is our choice but nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you trigger it, then there is a reciprocal obligation on your part. That may be a tactical -- but that is your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are entitled to take that posture under the rules and I believe should not be penalised for doing so. It should not justify other conduct which may be designed to obtain a tactical advantage by the Prosecution. Now the second issue was we can simply see the delay. I submit the prosecution knows, since last fall, we have consistently sought the earliest possible date for trial in this matter. Our client has been in custody for over a year. He has not had fresh air since January of this year. We have to seek the first possible trial date, and the Prosecution knows it is not an option for us to seek a two or three-month delay to further investigate documents that we may receive on the eve of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But is the proper preparation of defence not your first priority?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For any defence counsel, your Honour, there is a tension between extending your client's period of incarceration and preparing for trial, and we face very hard choices in that regard, but in all candour, we must press for the earliest trial date. Our client -- for our client to maintain his physical and mental condition, when he has not had fresh air since January of this year, is a very, very important consideration for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr Hayman, but now you can see why I very much wanted this matter to be handled by the other Trial Chamber, because we really do not want to involve ourselves in the issues that relate to trial, but I understand. Your client, you say, has been prejudiced because of the prosecution's tactical decision to seek a subpoena. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In fact, Trial Chamber 1 rebuffed the Prosecutor's earlier attempt in our case to proceed ex parte with respect to certain matters pertaining to witness anonymity. They do not acknowledge that that had any influence over their decision to come to this Trial Chamber, but nonetheless those are facts. So we, therefore, do believe that there is certainly a potential, if not an actual, violation of Article 21 with respect to unequal access of subpoenas and I wish to state that because of the earlier commentary concerning our desires to participate. I would like to mention one other matter, and that is in the brief of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated 25th March 1997, there is reference at the bottom of the first page: "A Memorandum of Understanding regarding cooperation between the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Prosecutor of this Tribunal". Then a quote is made from that Memorandum of Understanding. The defence has a concern in the case of General Blaskic that the parties do have dramatically unequal access to evidence, and that stems, of course, from the fact that, unlike any other international tribunal in history, this Tribunal is not affiliated with an occupying power that occupies the terrain of the conflict, nor does it have an army that answers to itself to collect evidence or otherwise take action. Therefore, the prosecution is working very closely with the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to collect evidence. I am not suggesting that is inappropriate, but they have an agreement, a Memorandum of Understanding, that governs the collection of evidence. We have asked the Prosecutor for it. We have been denied access to that Memorandum, and that exacerbates the defence's concerns that Article 21 may be being violated in an on-going matter. They have a secret agreement, at least secret from the defence, as to the manner in which they will collect and gain access to evidence and witnesses and bring them here before the Tribunal, because this document has been referenced in a brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Because this document has been referenced in a brief, we would ask that it be filed with the court and served upon us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Hayman. Does the Prosecutor have anything to say in this regard, as Judge Jan and Judge Odio Benito have told me this is a matter that really should be considered by the other Trial Chamber? I am not involved in that trial. If you wish to respond, you may. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Thank you, your Honour. I simply wish to state that this is not within the ambit of the issues that are before this Chamber this morning as to which Chamber should ultimately be seized of these kinds of issues. I have no comment at this stage, but it is clearly not within the ambit of the issue that we are to be addressed by this Chamber this morning, and I would certainly submit we should stay away from trying to resolve these issues at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The defence subpoena will be handled by Judge Jan ex parte as soon as we conclude these proceedings. Now, we will hear from Mr Rivkin or is it the Ambassador? Mr Simonovic? Presentation by MR SIMONOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: When you asked me yesterday, your Honour, whether I am an attorney or not, I said I was not, which correctly reflects my position. So I shall be only giving political and legal statement about the position of the Government of Croatia concerning admissibility of subpoena, and afterwards I will give the floor to special legal counsellors of the Government of Croatia. We will be having Miss Kate Baragona speaking and Mr Ivo Josipovic, our expert on criminal procedural law. Concerning the statement of the Republic of Croatia, it tries to emphasise three main points related to subpoena duces tecum. First, that subpoena duces tecum is not founded either on statute nor on international law; secondly, that it is unnecessary; and thirdly, that it is harmful. Presenting this statement, I shall be rather closely bound by my instructions, but I would be more than happy if there would be any questions on which I could elaborate the statement, because, apart from being Ambassador, I am also a law professor. So if you allow me, your Honour, I would like to proceed with the statement. The Republic of Croatia was one of the States that sought the establishment of this Tribunal and it will continue to support it. Furthermore, Croatia considers that it has both a moral and a legal obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal. We are appreciative of the resources that the international community has committed to the Tribunal so far, and we welcome the efforts of the Tribunal and its officials and support the Tribunal in its noble task. We will insist, however, that the Tribunal must function in a fair and equitable way, and especially that justice is dispensed by it within the framework set by existing international law and practice. The fact that Croatia appears before this Tribunal today expressing its objection to a particular action taken by the Prosecutor does not reflect Croatia's opposition to the Tribunal. On the contrary, our appearance has the sole purpose of assisting the Tribunal to find the way to adopt the right decision in a very sensitive matter, a decision which will simultaneously enable the Tribunal to carry out its mandate and facilitate the development of international criminal law. Now, your Honour, let me pass to our arguments against the subpoena, the first being that the subpoena is not founded neither in Statute nor in international law. The Tribunal and its enabling Statute were established by Resolutions of the United Nations Security Council. The function of the Statute is to define the boundaries of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. It is only within these bounds that the Tribunal is able to create its Rules of Procedure and Evidence. These bounds, as we shall demonstrate convincingly, should not and cannot include the subpoena. The Statute enabled the court to adopt the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the purpose of which is only to address technical questions of the administration of the Tribunal. In this regard I recall the words of the President of the Court, the honourable Judge Cassese, who in his address to the United Nations General Assembly on 19th November 1996 stated: "No rule of procedure, nor any amendment of such rules, may infringe the principles laid down in Statute." In considering the competence of the Tribunal, one ought to turn to two sources: the Statute and the statements made in the Security Council at the time of the adoption of Resolutions 808 and 827, the former creating the Tribunal and the latter defining its competencies through the Statute. These are the only authentic records on the questions of jurisdiction. The Statute is silent in respect of the mandate of the Tribunal on the issue of subpoena. Indeed, if the Statute in its entirety is construed properly, it is abundantly clear that the Tribunal does not have the power to issue subpoenas against sovereign states. In that regard, if the Security Council wanted the Tribunal to have such an extraordinary mandate, a mandate that would create a new practice in international law in dealing with states, it would certainly have stated that very clearly. However, exactly to the contrary, many Security Council members were explicit that they wanted to exclude the possibility of the creation of any creative innovations to international law by the Tribunal. I will quote some of them. The statement of the Venezuelan delegate upon the adoption of Resolution 827 includes the following explicit remarks: "The Tribunal as a subsidiary organ of the Council would not be empowered with nor would the Council be assuming the ability to set down norms of international law or legislate with respect to those rights. It simply applies existing international humanitarian law." The delegate of the United Kingdom said: "The Statute does not, of course, create new law, but reflects existing international law in this field." The New Zealand delegate was equally clear: "We must remember, however, that the Tribunal is a court. Its task is to apply independently and impartially the rules of customary international law, and we believe conventional law applicable in the territory of the former Yugoslavia." The Secretary General stated in his report to the Security Council of 3rd May 1993, to which the draft stated is attached: "It should be pointed out that in assigning to the International Tribunal the task of prosecuting persons for serious violations of international humanitarian law, the Security Council would not be creating or purporting to legislate that law. Rather, the International Tribunal would have the task of applying existing international humanitarian law." Unfortunately the Prosecutor in seeking the issuance of the subpoena in issue here is asking the Tribunal to engage in conduct that contravenes both the Statute and customary international law. The concept of subpoena does not exist in neither the Statute nor in international law. If one were to insist on this new legal practice, one would need to apply it in respect of all states equally, because of the principle of sovereign equality of states. That is the basic premise of the Charter and international law. Furthermore, Croatia cannot accept the use of subpoena in respect of its state officials. According to both the Statute and to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the states have the obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal and not particular governmental bodies, nor particular officials. All national laws, not only Croatia's, prohibit the dissemination of state documents by its officials without the prior approval of relevant state bodies. While, it is true that states must cooperate with the Tribunal, the state itself alone decides which is the relevant body that will carry out the businesses of cooperation with the Tribunal. A request for documentation or assistance from particular state officials that would violate internal laws on the use of state documents is not only contrary to international law, but it also threatens the internal legal organisation. When a Tribunal needs certain documents or when it requires other forms of cooperation from Croatia, it should communicate those requests through the government office for cooperation with the Tribunal. Requests that are submitted through other channels are not obligatory to Croatia because they contravene international law and violate the internal order of Croatia. No responsible government can accept a situation where the state is by-passed or ignored. Your Honour, let me pass to our second argument. Our second argument is that subpoena is unnecessary. Croatia, as any other state, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ambassador. Did you indicate that you wish to respond to questions or should I address those to Mr Rivkin or Miss Baragona?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I make a suggestion, your Honour, either of us will be happy to respond to any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: If I may clarify, your Honour, we are not having the problem which is related to communication of the Tribunal to Croatian authorities, so if you address us, we will be happy to answer on any level that you would prefer. If questions are related to this statement of government, I will be more than happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Before you go on then to your next point, I have a few questions. One, you indicated that when the Security Council established the Tribunal, it was not creating law but it was following the law that existed at that time. So it was not creating law. It was merely applying the existing law. My question is: what precedent did the Security Council have with respect to (a) the establishment of a judicial institution under Chapter 7; and (b) the establishment of a judicial institution under Chapter 7 which is criminal in nature? What were the norms that existed at that time with respect to those two considerations?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour,it is very obvious that we are facing something brand new with very little experience. We are also facing problems related to competencies of the court, to the importance of the court, which arise from differences in comparative law which exists in the United States, in the United Kingdom and Continental legal systems. I do agree with you certainly that the court is being something new and in that sense there will certainly be innovations, but I do not think that it is acceptable that such innovation can include the creation of new rules of international law. So when we are creating the court, it needs to have some flexibility. It needs to be efficient, but within the framework of limits of international criminal law, and concerning subpoena we do not have a single precedent in the history of the courts when subpoena is being issued by international tribunal to states, and there were international tribunals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Rivkin, at some point you can follow up or if you wish to add now. Probably you do not want to interrupt your presentation. Ambassador, how do you wish to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: For me it is perfectly convenient if Mr Rivkin has something to add and if you would allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Being a lawyer, I wanted to clarify something which sounded like a technicality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: He is a professor of international law. We need their guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I think the key point that the Ambassadors of Croatia are trying to make is not that the creation of the Tribunal by a Security Council was not an exceptional practice and certainly not a very important decision by the Security Council, but the Security Council did not want the Tribunal to create new international law. This is a fundamental difference that I think we are trying to draw here. If I may just add another quote here from the delegate of the United Kingdom: "The Statute does not, of course, create new law but reflects existing international law in this field." Again, as we will elaborate later on in your case in chief and my supplementary remarks, the Security Council almost has a plenary power to create all sorts of innovations, but only the Security Council, not necessarily this Tribunal, and certainly it was not the intention of the Security Council to vest the power in you to create new law. So that is really the distinctive belief we are trying to draw. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I ask a question? The Security Council has created an institution and given it a task of a judicial nature, and it has also permitted it to frame its own rules and procedures, etc. Now if the Tribunal, the institution, is not in a position to obtain evidence, then how can it perform its function which it has been entrusted with by the Security Council, because some sort of a summons, some sort of an order, some sort of a subpoena has to be issued in order to collect the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, we are going to address those issues at great length in our presentation. Permit me just to say at this time two things very briefly. Number one, I understand the argument of effectiveness and efficiency. We do believe that before you get to this point you need to look broadly at what is the overall ambit of powers given to this Tribunal or to any other body that is not a plenary body of a sovereign, but exists on the basis of a limited grant of power from another body. Once you establish that ambit of powers, all the other statutory tools apply. You cannot do it backwards. Secondly, as a factual matter, we do not see the situation as being a zero sum game, your Honour, where if you do not have a subpoena duces tecum power, you have no ability to function at all. In fact, I think facts speak for themselves. You have been functioning quite successfully, and I certainly would not presume to argue otherwise. You have indicted a number of people. You were conducting other investigations, and I believe you have convicted at least one individual. That is not certainly not an indicia of judicial paralysis. Again, if I may, we will address those issues at great length in our subsequent presentation. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Even investigators have to be given some sort of a power to collect evidence. Similarly the defence has to collect evidence in order to clear the position of the client. As was remarked by my learned sister judge, it is a new institution and therefore probably new international law rules will have to be created in order to make it official, so it does not become impotent. If you cannot issue any order for the collection of evidence, if you cannot issue any subpoena to ask for documents, then it is an entirely impotent institution and I do not think the Security Council has done its exercise in futility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me. Your questions are trying to draw out the thrust of our presentation. If you indulge us, we beg to defer so Ambassador Simonovic can continue his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ambassador, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. In fact, my second issue is just related to what His Honour was asking. The point we will argue is that a subpoena is unnecessary. Croatia, as any other state, is obliged to obey the request of the Tribunal. Why then does the Tribunal require subpoena? Certainly not because of efficacy. Because the subpoena is deemed to become no use anyhow, because there is no sanction provided explicitly for subpoena. Even if subpoena were issuable under international law against states, it would be considered no use since no sanction exists in support of it. To put it simply, the subpoena is not only unlawful but useless and unnecessary as well. The only available sanction for not complying with the requests of the Tribunal as set out in the Statute and Rules is notification of the Security Council which has a set of sanctions at its disposal. The same and nothing more can be a sanction. However, it should be noted that this step relates to the serious allegation of not cooperating with the Tribunal and is not available to be used as a substitute for what are perceived to be procedural deficiencies. Croatia agrees that the Tribunal should be efficient and that it should have teeth which can bite, if necessary, but there is no need to invent false and unlawful teeth that will bite and hurt the international orders. Your Honour, let me now pass to our third argument, very important in the future argument that subpoena is harmful. The application of the subpoena is harmful, because, first, it violates sovereignty of states. It is offensive, and it increased the resistance against cooperation of respective states with the Tribunal. Secondly, it creates new legal practice, which will raise suspicions and make creation of the permanent international criminal court more difficult and less likely. Should a tribunal step out of the bounds of its jurisdiction and find in favour of the prosecution, that is if the Tribunal empowered itself to step beyond the bounds of its own jurisdiction and existing international law by finding the subpoena valid and enforceable, it would be counter-productive to its relations with states and also the future development of the international criminal jurisdiction. The creation of a new legal practice in this instance would have far-reaching impact upon the present international order, which is based on a clear definition of sovereignty and the position of state. The possibility that states could be requested to make available state secrets will have negative impact upon the further development of international criminal jurisprudence, since states shall be unwilling to support such developments. In this context we note that during the preparations for the establishment of a permanent international criminal court the subpoena has not even been discussed as a possibility, because it could infringe on or violate the sovereignty principle, and it is, therefore, unacceptable to states. Furthermore, the argument raised in the submission of the prosecution about so-called culprit states upon whom such claims can be made and other states against whom they cannot creates different categories of states. The introduction of such a concept to international law would, first, produce international outrage and be objected to by most and especially small states, and, secondly, have a negative impact upon the evolving process of the development of permanent international criminal court, to which this Tribunal should otherwise give significant impetus. In establishing and protecting sovereignty, Croatia has had too many victims and has given enormous sacrifices. Its citizens will not tolerate to be treated as citizens of a second class state nor a culprit state according to the criteria proposed by the submission of the prosecution. This idiom, a "culprit state", is especially disturbing when referring to Croatia, a state that was a victim of aggression itself and a state that helped Bosnia-Herzegovina survive. Your Honour, after elaborating on three major arguments against subpoena, that it is not founded in Statute and in international law in general, in fact that it is against it, that it is unnecessary because states are obliged to cooperate with the court anyhow, and that there is a clear, legally grounded way to sanction their lack of cooperation, if necessary, and, finally, that it is harmful, because it is irritating at least some states that should cooperate with the Tribunal, and because it makes the establishment of the international criminal court less likely, let me conclude. It is tempting for the Tribunal, including the honourable judge, to support the issue of the subpoena, especially taking into account that the Tribunal have issued two of them already. It requires strength and capability to view matters within a broader perspective, to resist such a temptation. I believe that the Tribunal is powerful enough to resist such a temptation. The greatest majority of amici curiae have been presenting rather similar or the same views as the Republic of Croatia. However there are a few participants at this hearing who would like its outcome to represent a new step in the development of the international criminal law. Some amici curiae who are here, who have come not as typical representatives of the legal systems and of international law and international criminal law, but as persons motivated to participate and contribute to the creation of something new, perhaps a new precedent and a new legal practice in international law. The real issue is that the Tribunal must not create a dangerous precedent, a dangerous new practice, since it would be contrary to international law, unnecessary and harmful. Instead, it should reject the temptation and reject the use of subpoena. The Tribunal, in our view, should continue with well-balanced steps rooted in existing international law and stay within the framework of the established international organ. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just before you finish, has the government of Croatia nominated any functionary or authority through which the request of the Tribunal for production of documents, production of witnesses, can be routed, because you said it should not be sent to the state or state officials --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- but the state authority designated by the government. Have you designated a particular officer or particular dignitary through whom these requests for production of documents, production of witnesses can be routed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have passed a constitutional law on cooperation of Croatia with the Tribunal, and within this law there is an explicit provision concerning the establishment of the office for cooperation. The head of the office is appointed, has his name and is sitting right here, and it is clearly an identifiable person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The obligation to cooperate does not belong to the office, does it? It belongs to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In Article 2 of your Constitutional Act you provide: "On behalf of the Republic of Croatia, the Government of the Republic of Croatia shall be the co-ordinator of the cooperation with the Tribunal." Later on you do mention the office -- I cannot find it. Let us see. In any case, the obligation to cooperate rests with Croatia, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: With the office. The head of the office is Mr Jelanic, who is not here. You have indicated he is in the gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: He is in the gallery. Constitution law provides government to establish an office for cooperation and it has established an office for cooperation. Certainly the obligations are not obligations of individuals. Those are obligations of state, and the state has a status of an organisation which is in charge of distributing powers to individual offices. So representing a state we have an office created by the government and having high government officials, as a council of the office fully responsible even for the harder decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I presume Professor Jelanic does not have the authority to act in a way that the Government of Croatia would not approve?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly he is acting in accordance with the laws of Croatia and it is a governmental office. In the Council there are a couple of vice presidents of government and ministers of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have no additional questions, Ambassador Simonovic. Thank you very much for responding to our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Presentation by MS BARAGONA

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Madam President, may it please the Tribunal, I have been asked to address several points of international and domestic law in addition to those made by His Excellency Ambassador Simonovic. First, the prosecution seeks an unusual form of process in a subpoena duces tecum that is not recognised under international law or the law of most states other than the United States and even then in a form that would not be available under American law. Second, neither the Tribunal's Statute nor its Rules for Procedure and Evidence properly construed allow for the use of subpoena duces tecum against a state or its officials. Third, the Prosecutor seeks to sanction Croatian government officials who are not subject to the Tribunal's jurisdiction in their individual capacities, and not subject to sanction in their official capacities. Significantly these points implicate every United Nations member state, this Tribunal, as well as others in future international tribunals. It should be clearly recognised here that the power claimed by the Prosecutor to issue compulsory process to the Republic of Croatia and to sanction its officials for failure to comply, if accepted by this Tribunal, may be applied to each and every state in turn. Thus, the proper disposition of this issue is of enormous importance to the future of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs Baragona. I do not think the prosecution has taken the position that it has the authority or the Tribunal has the authority to impose a penal sanction on a state. They do take the position that the Tribunal may issue a subpoena, but may only impose a penal sanction on individuals. Do you feel that the mere denomination of the document as a subpoena is somehow a sanction that exceeds the power of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are discussing primarily the form of this request. I think, as the Ambassador has mentioned, the Croatian Government has no objection to the cooperation which is explicitly stated in the Rules. What it does have objection to is the form of a subpoena to be issued against a sovereign state. We are not even discussing the use of a subpoena by the Tribunal as against individual persons in their private capacities. We are discussing the use of a subpoena, in this case a subpoena duces tecum, as regards a sovereign state, and then that subsequent application of subpoena to its high government officials merely on the basis of their capacity as officials and from that also applying or expressing an ability to oppose a sanction against that official for failure to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is a different issue. If we can just remain with the first issue, the Tribunal does have authority to issue orders to states.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: We do not dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And states have a duty to comply.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: We do not dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Tribunal has the authority to make a determination that there has been non-compliance and report it to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, we do not concede that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That itself would be a penalty, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: We believe so, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do not want the document to go to the state to be entitled a subpoena. It appears to me it is more of a political-type argument. You were not present when we were discussing the Bosnia-Herzegovina subpoena. Perhaps Miss Glumac can enlighten you. The suggestion was made by the individual that if I wrote him a letter, perhaps he would come. That is in a sense form over substance and telling the Trial Chamber and the Tribunal how it should exercise its power. Just because a party is offended because we use the word "subpoena", if we make the determination that the subpoena will not result in a penalty to be imposed by the Tribunal, that is unfortunate, but the duty is to comply.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think that Croatia is offended. It is not an emotional response. This is a technical response to a legal term of art. Subpoena, if it becomes acceptable in international law as something that is applicable to sovereign states, the development in the Bosnian situation that: "We did not really mean it to have any penalties" might not be carried forward. In the future a subpoena duces tecum would be applied as against sovereign states. We, the Croatian Government, feel that that form is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Does Croatia possess sufficient sovereignty so as not to be bound to comply with an order issued by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: If they invoke the exception of state secrets, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Otherwise they are -- otherwise they have explicitly agreed to be bound to cooperate and have that duty under the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: That was merely my introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Tell us some more.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Okay. Item 1: the Tribunal's power to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a state or its officials. The Prosecutor seeks an extraordinary power that is unavailable under most legal systems other than that of the United States, and in a form that would neither be legal nor constitutional in the context of a criminal Prosecution in the United States. However, the Prosecutor cannot point to any principle of international law or any provision of a Statute establishing this Tribunal, or to its Rules of Procedure and Evidence that expressly allow the issuance of a subpoena duces tecum against a state or its officials. Rather, she would have the Tribunal believe that this is a routine power inherent in all courts and therefore properly executed by this one. This is untrue. The subpoena duces tecum is not a well-accepted conventional device available routinely in the world's courts. In fact, it is a concept that is unknown in most legal systems. The subpoena duces tecum is primarily an American innovation, written in the very broad discovery provisions of the United States Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. Application of the subpoena duces tecum in the international forum is highly controversial, and a number of states have, in fact, adopted working statutes which prohibit the domestic application of these American-style discovery orders. Some of these states include, for example, the Netherlands, France, Sweden, the United Kingdom and Canada, some of the very same states the prosecution is quoting as being in support of the position that a subpoena duces tecum is available as against a sovereign state. The international application of American-style discovery rules and particularly the subpoena duces tecum is properly controversial. The subpoena duces tecum is a device that is specifically tailored to operate in the American legal system. It operates in conjunction with all the statutory and constitutional limitations on the powers of the court and the prosecutors in the United States, including the 4th Amendment of the US Constitution, which prohibits unreasonable searches and seizures and when directed against government officials, the fundamental separation of power principles enshrined in that document. The Prosecutor would have this court import this very unique American procedure into international law, but without the legal and constitutional limitations that restrict its use even in the United States. Moreover, the subpoena duces tecum in the broad civil form that the Prosecutor seeks here is not available even in the United States. This is a criminal tribunal. It has the authority to try criminal indictments, indictments for the most serious possible crimes, and to impose punishments up to and including life imprisonment. In such situations the United States Supreme Court has made it unequivocally clear that the subpoena duces tecum available under the US Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure cannot be used as the Prosecutor would use it in this case as a discovery device designed to collect any potentially relevant information. In the US case The United States v Nixon, the court explained that a subpoena duces tecum sought in a criminal case cannot be used as a general fishing expedition. Rather, the subpoena duces tecum in a criminal case under the federal rules is a very limited, narrowly tailored process for requiring the production of documents before trial. Interestingly, the Prosecutor cites the Federal Rules of Procedure, 17, which describes the use of subpoena but does not go further to Rule 17(H) which says: "Statements by witnesses or prospective witnesses may not be subpoenaed from the Government or the defendant under this rule." In the Nixon case, which involved a subpoena duces tecum issued to the President of the United States seeking certain specific documents -- in that case tape recordings of the President and defendants -- the Supreme Court ruled that a Prosecutor must meet a number of specific requirements before the production of documents can be compelled. As the court wrote: "A Prosecutor must show that the documents are evidentiary and relevant, that they are not otherwise procurable reasonably in advance of the trial by the exercise of due diligence, that the party cannot properly prepare for trial without such production and inspection in advance of trial, and that the failure to obtain such inspection may tend unreasonably to delay the trial, and that the application is made in good faith and not intended as a general fishing expedition." In other words, in order to carry the burden, a Prosecutor must clear three hurdles: relevancy, admissibility and specificity. Thus, with respect to each and every document sought by the Prosecutor, she must show that it will contain evidence admissible with respect to the offences charged in the indictment. In this case the Prosecutor has not even attempted to establish that the documents she seeks might contain relevant evidence, let alone evidence that would be clearly admissible at trial. She is, in fact, your Honours, embarking on exactly the kind of fishing expedition which was forbidden in the Nixon case. Therefore, despite the Prosecutor's assurances that she merely is seeking to invoke a well-established practice available to all courts and thus by inference available to this Tribunal, she is actual plea arguing for the importation of a unique American-style practice into international law in an unlimited form that is unknown even in the United States, and indeed in a form which is fundamentally inconsistent with the American Constitution and the established rules governing in criminal procedure. We urge the Tribunal to reject this assertion of power. Item 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Before you leave the United States procedure -- I thought I left that behind me, but let us talk about it a little bit. First of all, you say that it is not applicable in criminal proceedings in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: In the broad sense being sought by the Prosecutor in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Of course, there is a different circumstance, is there not, because at least in terms of sovereignty what we have in this institution is being established under Chapter 7 of the UN Charter; there is already a waiver of sovereignty by the member states because they give the Security Council primary authority to make the determination as to whether behaviour is a threat to peace and to make the determination under 24 -- whatever the rule is -- to determine the appropriate measures. So there is already a waiver of sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Vis-a-vis the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Vis-a-vis the Security Council, but, of course, we do have the authority, as you have indicated, to issue orders that must be complied with and a state cannot say: "We are sovereign."

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, I did not say that, your Honour. They can respond: "We are sovereign and this is a state secret"; yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us leave that aside for a moment. Of course they can object on the basis of national secrets and in a moment we will talk about how that might be dealt with as a general principle, absent the invocation of a state secret privilege, they cannot waive sovereignty and say: "We will not comply because we are sovereign."

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may add, your Honour, we are not arguing, much as some of us might prefer it, that your procedures are governed by the American Constitution, although I think that may not be a big problem as far as your Honour is concerned. The whole purpose of elucidating the American-style procedure is because it is our impression, and -- correct us if we are wrong -- having read the Prosecutor's brief, that the Prosecutor is trying very hard to convince your Honours that the very style of the process, the form of the process is a routine device, and we believe it is very instructive for this court to hear our view (a) that it is not a routine device; and (b) that even in the very jurisdiction, the mother load, if you will, of that process which she is seeking would never fly. From that perspective we will be happy to discuss Nixon or any other case, but we are certainly not supporting a proposition that this Tribunal is bound by American Constitution or American case law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think if Miss Baragona can respond in this respect, it might make it easier, and then when you have your opportunity, we will talk to you. I suppose my point was: when you say it is unknown even in the United States, then what you meant is that it is unknown that the national security privilege cannot be raised as a bar to the subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not particularly referring to that when I was saying the use of the subpoena duces tecum was unknown -- was unavailable as a tool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is unavailable because it is separation of powers. What I am suggesting is that we have a different situation here, because what we have now at least is a body that was created by the Security Council under Chapter 7, and the issue of sovereignty or when you want to say analogously separation of powers does not have a place in this proceeding, nor does it have a place in any judicial institution that is treaty based. With respect to irrelevance, you stated that there are three standards: relevance, admissibility and specificity. Of course the documents must be admissible but need they be relevant or must they just lead to evidence that must be relevant or should we be concerned with that since that is a American rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I think I agree with your latter statement. I am not in a position to say what the court should be reviewing or what rules or what thought processes it would be applying when it was determining the relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: When you say that subpoenas may not -- that statements may not be subpoenaed, that may be true under certain circumstances, but of course, in the United States statements are given to the prosecution under the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure after a witness testifies. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are not saying that the Croatian Government would not give documents and would not give statements. We are objecting to the tool being requested by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Because the federal rules of criminal procedure explicitly provide that statements in criminal proceedings will not be the subject of discovery prior to the witness testifying. So there is an explicit rule in the American system that they are not required to be produced -- statements -- prior to the witness testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We do not have a rule like that, do we?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, you do not but you do not also have the rule which was 17(C) which the Prosecutor cited if support of her proposition that the subpoena duces tecum was available. My only point in that, referring to 17(H) in addition to 17(C), was to point out that the Prosecutor is taking tools out of context for her own purposes and not fully informing in her brief what the real rule is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What the limitations are.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: What the limitations are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I understand. With respect to Reynolds and Nixon, do these cases stand for the proposition that there is an absolute bar to the production of documents that may contain national secrets, or does it stand for the proposition that the responding party must make a showing that -- a facie showing -- it does not use the term prima facie -- an initial showing that they are, in fact, national secrets, and that under certain circumstances may be enough so that the court will not receive those documents itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there is some truth in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I think there is a correctness in both statements that you made. Nixon does not stand for the proposition that documents from the sovereign government are unavailable. There must be a balancing. I am speaking to this subject later, but that balancing in the particular case was a balancing made by two organs of the same sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: This is a different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Protected by the notion of separation of powers and a question of just how far the judiciary can impede into the province of the executive branch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes. I think by reference to this situation, we say how far can the judicial Tribunal impede into the sovereignty of the state to make its own determination, its own balance of whether the state security interests are somehow not to the level of the Tribunal's interest in concluding to a fair and just end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder whether that is an appropriate fit, because what we have here is a body, the International Tribunal, that is given primacy because of the powers that flow from Chapter 7, and sovereignty really is -- I do not see it as an issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Primacy over national law but not primacy over the sovereignty of a country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Primacy in so far as states have a duty to cooperate, primacy in so far as they have a duty to defer to the jurisdiction of this Tribunal if there is an on-going procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Respectfully I think primacy is used in a different context, your Honour. By objecting to the use of the term "primacy" I am not saying that the Government of Croatia does not have a duty to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think you are right. "Primacy" is used in a context of the relationship between our proceedings and the proceedings of another state.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You are correct, but they do have a duty, though that flows from Chapter 7 to comply with the orders of the Tribunal because we are an enforcement measure. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. But national secrets then. In terms of the way that national secrets then are handled even by a tribunal, by our Tribunal as opposed to a federal court in the United States, there may be different considerations there, because you do not have --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I think they are very different, your Honour. I think it is of a difficult analogy to say that the Tribunal, which is an international body, which does not answer to the people of the sovereign state, nor represent the sovereign state -- it is difficult to say that that Tribunal is in the same position to judge the national security interest of a sovereign state as is another organ of that same sovereign state to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So you say we are in a lesser position and we should give greater deference to the states in the assertion of their national interest privilege.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, because I believe that there is a tool available to the Tribunal if they are unhappy with such a situation. They have refer it to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Which will then exercise its political judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Its plenary powers, given to it by that sovereign state. On to item 2. The Prosecutor seeks to exercise power that the Security Council has not granted to the Tribunal. The Prosecutor's claim that the Security Council vested this Tribunal with express power to issue a subpoena duces tecum to states and to officials also is untrue. Her brief fails to point to any language in the Tribunal's founding Statute that expressly grants it such authority. Rather, she seeks the Tribunal to infer an express grant, itself a contradiction in terms, from the Tribunal's Statute and Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The provisions the Prosecutor invokes, however, neither expressly nor by implication give the Tribunal the power to issue a subpoena duces to a state or its officials. Under the Tribunal's Statute, the obligation of a state like Croatia is to cooperate with and assist Tribunal. Emphatically the Statute does not give the Tribunal general authority to prosecute or judge states. In undertaking the obligation to cooperate with and assist the Tribunal, neither Croatia nor any other state has agreed to carry out the Tribunal's orders without question regardless of whether they are consistent with established international law and practice. The Tribunal's relationship to states is, in fact, carefully delineated in the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last sentence again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: In undertaking the obligation to cooperate with and assist the Tribunal, neither Croatia nor any other state has agreed to carry out the Tribunal's orders without question regardless of whether they are consistent with established international law and practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So they have to sit in judgement upon the judgement of the Tribunal. That is what you intend there?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Respectfully what I would say is like any counsel or any party involved in a question before a Tribunal, there are challenges to procedure which are available to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Certainly you can criticise a judgement. After a judgement is delivered, it becomes public property.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A judgement delivered of course is public property. It can be criticised but it has to be carried out but what you are saying is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I am saying that a state which has agreed to cooperate with and assist this Tribunal still has a right to make objections when they feel that they are just, appropriate and necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What is the analogue for this Tribunal in international law? In your brief you say that the Prosecutor can point to no judicial institution that has the power to issue subpoenas and what they do is refer to other international judicial institutions, all of which are without that power, and I think you are correct, but is there an analogue? Can we go to court X that existed in international law and say: "Here is a court that existed in international law and that does not have a subpoena power?". Is there an analogue in international law?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: We all agree, your Honour: the answer is the International Court of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I do not know whether everyone would agree. That is fine. In the International Court of Justice, as I pointed out yesterday -- I do not have it with me -- the Article of the Charter provides that there is a duty to resort to the Security Council for enforcement. So in creating the International Court of Justice there it was determined that you must go to the Security Council if there is a need for enforcement. There is nothing in that Statute, and you would think that the drafters of our Statute, knowing what they said in the Charter as it relates to the International Court of Justice, that if they wanted to make that requirement, they could have taken their pen and copied the language directly from the Charter. They did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I think that issue was addressed in one of the amici briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Probably not to my satisfaction. You tell me about it. Article 94 says: "If any party to a case fails to perform the obligations incumbent upon it under a judgement rendered by the court, the other party may have recourse to the Security Council, which may, if it deems necessary, make recommendations or decide upon measures to be taken to give effect in the judgement." We have a principle, do we not, even in international law -- I mean in American law -- I do not remember what it is -- maybe one of the scholars can tell us about it -- that by omitting that reference perhaps it was intended that it not apply to this court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, two comments. An analogue does not mean an exact replica and equal situation. There will be points that are similar and points that are dissimilar. As regards the second, it is known in more common law systems that that which is not prohibited is allowed, but under civil law that which is not allowed is prohibited. Now, we could get into a very lengthy discussion regarding whether common law's principle or civil law's principle is the more appropriate one to apply for this International Tribunal, but I am at this point not prepared to do that in a sufficient manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Statute itself -- well, that may not be a fair question -- is more common law than it is civil law, the Statute creating the Tribunal? It has attributes of both so that is not really...

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I have to say, your Honour, I do not think I am in a position to answer that question. I would point out, though, that two-thirds of the world's judicial bodies are civil law. So the balance of legal weight would be on the side of civil law, which says that which is not allowed is prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may supplement, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine. One other question before I forget. I would appreciate if you would provide me with cites to the blocking statutes that you referred to on page 7 of your brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: We shall do so, your Honour. I think it might be instructive to elaborate in this instance we clearly believe it is a civil law situation. Again I will get into it in greater detail in my remarks. Very briefly, with all due respects to your Honours, you are a Tribunal with much limited, very important, very awesome powers, but limited powers. Therefore we believe the proper proposition is the absence of a specific language creating some power is exclusive but is definitive proof that you do not have this power. It would be absurd in that statutory situation to enumerate all of them but, briefly, your Statute does not indicate that you have the power to send out snatch squads or command military force to accomplish your objectives. I mean, one can think about thousands of different powers that you do not have. It would have been absurd for Security Council to set them all out in explicit detail. Their absence with all due respect to your Honours, to us is proof you do not have a problem rather the reverse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: One last comment regarding your question about the analogy between the International Court of Justice and the Tribunal. The International Court of Justice is on an equal footing with the Security Council. This Tribunal is an auxiliary organ of the Security Council. That would suggest that there are some differences in the powers that are available to the two. In that situation it may be that the Security Council has that power, hence the Tribunal's need to go to the Security Council to have that power enforced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We are subsidiary, an independent body, Judge Odio Benito would say. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Which is a very good description. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: There is another important difference between the ICJ and this Tribunal. We are a penal Tribunal prosecuting persons who are detained in jail.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: ICJ is a court for states also. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Hypothetically speaking, it is very difficult to imagine how could this Tribunal prosecute fairly and expeditiously someone going every time to the Security Council, asking for the cooperation of states, hypothetically speaking. It is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in no way are we proposing that this Tribunal goes to the Security Council in every instance. We are only concerned with the very narrow area regarding the issuance of a tool such as the subpoena against a sovereign state. There are many instances where this Tribunal has no requirement to go to the Security Council. We are only saying that, in this particular instance, where this Tribunal feels that a member state has not cooperated, you then have the recourse of the Security Council. It is not that you have no recourse. It is that in this particular, narrow situation the remedy that is available is the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mrs Baragona. You were saying -- you were beginning to discuss your argument that there is no language in the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: The Tribunal's relationship to states is, in fact, carefully delineated in the Statute and is governed by Article 29 of that document. Article 29 requires all states to cooperate with the Tribunal, and provides that: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or an order issued by a trial chamber including but not limited to the taking of testimony and the production of evidence". The Prosecutor claims that this language gives the Tribunal the power to issue subpoenae duces tecum to statements, because it enjoins statements to comply with requests for assistance and orders issued by the court for production of evidence. This language, however, must be read in context. First, the types of orders actually named in Article 29 all address the problems of identifying, investigating, locating and arresting individual suspects. The full provision requires states to comply with requests for assistance and to comply with orders of the following type: the identification and location of persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Read the principal clause not including -- read the principal clause of this subsection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It says: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance issued by a Trial Chamber including but not limited to ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a general power, because when you use the word "including" it is extending --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Including these particular enumerated tools or these particular enumerated actions, all within the context of the problem of identifying, locating, investigating and locating, and arresting individual suspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But not limited to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Not limited to item 1 through 5 as regards the problem of identifying, locating, investigating and arresting suspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure many writers of statutes would agree with you on that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You are not saying that that is the sole obligation of states?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As it relates to the Tribunal, that is the sole obligation of being able to arrest and detain and transfer persons who are indicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Not even the sole responsibility, just so that it is illustrative of but not conclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Croatia has taken the position in its Statute, in its constitutional Act on cooperation with the International Tribunal in Article 25 that it will cooperate with the Tribunal in investigative measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: We do not disagree with that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is not something that they are doing because they want to; that is something that is part of their obligations under the Statute. Is that not so?
