utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor would interpret the language of item number 2, which states: "The taking of testimony and the production of evidence" to incorporate the issuance of a subpoena duces tecum merely because it refers to the production of evidence. She is unable, however, to cite any authority supporting the proposition that the Security Council intended to incorporate within the term "production of evidence" the very specific tool and process of a subpoena duces tecum against a state. As explained above, orders requiring the production of documents as a discovery device are not established international practice, nor are such orders routinely used the by all states in domestic disputes. Rather, the subpoena duces tecum is a device that is found in US civil and criminal procedure. There is, in fact, no evidence that the Security Council intended to incorporate within the Tribunal's Statute the US Federal Rules of Civil or criminal procedure or to invest the Tribunal with the power to issue all of the orders and process that a court in the United States, or any other international court for that matter, may issue. The Prosecutor's invocation of Article 19 of the Statute which gives the Tribunal the authority to issue: "Such orders and warrants for the arrest, detention, surrender or transfer of persons or any other order as may be required for the conduct of the trial"; and Article 15, which authorises the Tribunal to adopt the rules of procedure and evidence suffer from the same fatal flaw, as does the Prosecutor's invocation of Rule 54." Rule 54 allows the Tribunal to issue orders, summonses, subpoenas, warrants and transfer orders as may be necessary for the purpose of an investigation or the preparation or conduct of the trial. The rule does not, however, provide for the issuance of such process against a state, nor does it provide for the issuance of a subpoena duces tecum which, (discussed above) is an extraordinary process that is not an established international law procedure. Notably Rules 55 through 59 detail exactly how a state's cooperation may be sought to enforce orders issued pursuant to the general rule of 54. No provision is made for the issuance of binding process directed at a state, of which it is itself the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Rule 54 also provides for the issuance of orders: "Orders may be directed to states". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Transfer orders also provided in 54, those may be directed to states; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Warrants? Summonses? May they be directed to states?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Warrants are directed to a suspect and the state is asked to help execute it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So the warrant is sent to the state and we have unsuccessfully asked for states to cooperate in the execution of those warrants. Those then are directed to the state. Summonses, would those be directed to states for execution?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Everything mentioned in 54 you would agree are addressable to states except for subpoenas? You would say that that is because of the sovereign immunity of a state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us give Miss Baragona a chance. You will have an opportunity to supplement it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the subpoena may be issued for the purpose of investigating and the preparation or the conduct of the trial. The state's obligation is to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to Article 29, you have said that that really focuses on persons. I do not think I fully understand your argument, but I thought you were saying that it really focuses on a duty to cooperate with respect to turning over, surrendering, transferring persons, and is really a discovery device for the Prosecutor. Is that your argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my argument is much simpler than that. It is that the provisions are not made for the provision of binding process directed at the state. The Tribunal has these powers and the state has an obligation to cooperate. When the state in the view of the Tribunal has not fulfilled its obligation to cooperate, the Tribunal then is left to refer the matter to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Which is not provided for in the Statute, but you say is provided for in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But all of those Rules deal with -- 11, 59 and 61 all deal with situations that occur before the initial appearance, before the Trial Chamber begins the process of attempting to set an expeditious trial for an accused like General Blaskic, who is here. So we are in a different posture now, are we not? If the state had refused to execute an arrest warrant for co-counsel -- not co-counsel -- a co-defendant, for example, that may be one thing, but when we now have an individual in custody, do you not think that the tribunal has an overriding responsibility to provide, as is set forth in Article 20, I think, of the Statute, an expeditious trial -- fair and expeditious proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but that would not necessarily carry forward as to giving it a specific power for subpoena duces tecum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you not believe that criminal courts have inherent powers which are necessary for the proper conduct of their proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Within the limited scope of their limited jurisdiction and powers, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Limited scope of jurisdiction and their powers of course inherent by its very nature and by definition means it would not be set forth specifically but explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: What is inherent would be limited. It is not a situation where the Tribunal could infer whatever was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Right. You say it must be necessary and effective, and in truth that power is not necessary because we can go to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Here we are now with a person in custody for 12 months. You heard defence counsel, Mr Hayman, and saw him, and he is anxious for his client obviously to have a trial. If these records are necessary for a fair trial, we now are arguing with dozens of people about this, and then you would suggest that after we finish our discussion we write a letter to the Security Council and ask them to exercise their political judgement, as Mr Malanczuk said yesterday, as to whether or not they would allow us to continue with our judicial proceedings. Is that truly effective?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Would tailor it much more narrowly. I would not say that you would have to be -- that you would be unable to proceed. In every judicial forum there are limitations. There are points where the proceeding must be delayed because of important issues that have to be clarified. This subpoena issue, the subpoena duces tecum issue is one of those issues. From our position we are not doing this in any way to unduly delay the trial. We are doing this -- we are objecting because we feel that this is a fundamental point of international law, that this particular tool requested by the prosecution is unavailable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Unknown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It sure is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: And should not be applied as against a sovereign state or its high officials. We feel that that is important enough to be clarified before we proceed. It does not mean that the Prosecutor could not employ any other means available to her to continue to speak the very same information which she believes is important or necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And the defence also now has requested that a subpoena be issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me just a minute. Miss Baragona, you are doing fine. We will stand in recess for fifteen minutes. (11.30am) (Short break) (11.45 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Have you completed your submission, Miss Baragona?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: In truth, your Honours, the prosecution's appeal to what is undoubtedly the most threadbare and abusive prosecutorial tool known in law is actually an argument of necessity. The power to issue a subpoena duces tecum the prosecution claims is necessary for the effective performance of the Tribunal's function and therefore it must have it. If the Prosecutor is correct, of course, then the Tribunal has any and all power that might be considered necessary for the effective performance of its functions. Under the Prosecutor's reasoning, the Prosecutor could demand the Tribunal issue an order allowing it to use any measures necessary, legal or illegal, to obtain evidence she believes might be relevant to a particular prosecution. Indeed, the Prosecutor would be able to demand an order allowing for the kidnapping or torture of suspects or witnesses because this may be necessary for the effective performance of the Tribunal's function. This would be an unprecedented grant of power and of doubtful legality, and a grant that the Security Council neither made nor purported to make. We ask that the Tribunal firmly reject the Prosecutor's appeal to the justification of necessity. Even if the claim of necessity were legitimate, the Prosecutor has failed to show that any court, domestic or international, recognises the subpoena duces tecum in the broad, unlimited form she has requested. How can a power denied to most other courts be considered to be necessary for this Tribunal? In fact, the Prosecutor's real claim here is that this extraordinary power would be expedient; subverting the usual rules of law and process would, of course, always make any Prosecutor's job easier. Such claims, however, should have no standing in this or in any other criminal court, and should be rejected. Of course, if the Prosecutor is correct, then not only is Croatia subject to the subpoena duces tecum because this might be necessary, but each and every other state would be subject to the same process, regardless of their national security interests. In this record it is important to state that neither the Prosecutor nor the Tribunal are authorised by the Security Council, and neither are in a position to judge the national security needs or interests of Croatian or any other states. The right of states to decline a request for national security information is, in fact, well-established, and even the Prosecutor concedes that states may invoke the exception of national security. She incorrectly asserts, however, that Croatia's national security claims must be subject to the discretion of the Trial Chamber which has issued the subpoena duces tecum. To support this extraordinary claim, the Prosecutor cites numerous examples where the domestic courts of the state have required production of materials that are subject to a claim of national security, after weighing the claim against other competing interests in such a case. Such examples, however, are entirely opposite to the case where an international tribunal seeks such security information from a sovereign statement. In the case of a domestic dispute, the domestic court that waives the claim of national security is nevertheless a part of the state and the nation involved. The judges who make such decisions are part of the constituted legitimate government of such states, and ultimately are accountable either to higher government authority or to their fellow citizens for the decisions they make. The only issue in such cases is which institution or individual in the state in question is constitutionally empowered to speak definitively for the sovereign. Neither the Prosecutor nor the Tribunal can speak for Croatia or any other state and neither are in either sense accountable to the Croatian people. They cannot claim the right to determine what is or is not the national security interest of the Croatian people any more than they can claim to determine the national security interest of the people of the United States, Great Britain, France, Germany or any other sovereign state. Indeed, it is well settled practice for states in similar situations to refuse requests for assistance from international courts on the grounds of national security. Article 48 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice, for example, provides: "That the court shall make orders for the conduct of the case and make all arrangements connected with taking of evidence." Article 49 there allowed the court to call on the parties to produce any documents. However, the obligation of even party states to comply with such requests is limited. For example, the United Kingdom refused to supply certain documents to the International Court of Justice in the Corfu Channel case, in which it was a party, and it was not subject to sanction. There is no authority in international law or in reason that would support a different rule for Croatia. In her zeal, the Prosecutor also has asserted that Croatia, having once been incorporated into the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, has a special obligation to cooperate with whatever orders she may seek. This special obligation is found, the Prosecutor argues, from the Chapter 7 powers of the Security Council, which are: "Coercive vis a vis the culprit state or entity and only mandatory vis-à-vis the other member states." The Security Council has not and could not determine that the Republic of Croatia poses a threat to the peace, that it has caused a breach of the peace or that it is guilty of an act of aggression. It is not a culprit state, as the Prosecutor has implied. Although this is neither the time or the place to recount the factual basis of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, Croatia was and has been recognised by the international community, including the Security Council and several of its permanent members, as a victim of aggression. In any event, the powers attributable to the Security Council under Article 7 are uniquely within its special competence. It has the power to declare a sovereign state to be an international outlaw and to bring the full force of the international community, including military force, down upon it. These powers can be exercised only by a majority vote of the Council and is subject to veto by any one of the permanent members. They are not susceptible to exercise by the Prosecutor or by this Tribunal. Indeed, these vast powers are not judicial powers in any sense. These involve political, policy and military determinations that are inherently beyond the purview of any traditional body. Croatia has the obligation to assist the Tribunal that every other member state has, no more, no less. It has, in fact, cooperated with the Tribunal to the extent far in excess of other states involved. I would point out at this time that Croatia as we speak and meet here today is cooperating with requests from the Prosecutor to produce documents. Third and final point. The Tribunal does not have the authority to sanction a state official for failing to comply with the purported subpoena duces tecum. The Prosecutor claims that the Tribunal is empowered to sanction officials of the Government of the Republic of Croatia for failure to comply with the subpoena duces tecum. The Tribunal should also reject this claim. The Tribunal was created by the United Nations Security Council for a specific purpose and was endowed with specific limited authority to achieve that purpose. Under the Tribunal's founding Statute its competence is expressly stated and defined as follows: "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 in accordance with the provisions of the present Statute." Thus, in accordance with Article 1 of its Statute, the Tribunal's authority is limited to the prosecution of persons in accordance with the provisions of the Statute. The Statute provides no mechanism by which the Tribunal can independently sanction either a state or its officials for failing to comply with the purported subpoena duces tecum. The Tribunal has itself acknowledged this in its Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which do not purport to allow the sanctioning of a state for failing to comply with such a request. Indeed, where the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence do address the question of a state's failing to cooperate with the Tribunal, the Tribunal properly defers to the Security Council. For example, Rule 10 allows the Trial Chamber to issue a formal request to a state to defer domestic judicial proceedings concerning matters within the Tribunal's jurisdiction. If a state fails to comply with such a request, the Trial Chamber may request that the President report the matter to the Security Council. The same is true under Rule 13. Indeed, this is the standard international practice: "No international tribunal we are aware of has been granted powers to enforce any orders against sovereign states, including their own final judgements. The Prosecutor seeks to avoid this fundamental limit on the Tribunal's authority by seeking to sanction Croatian government officials as individuals. This too must fail. The Tribunal does not have general jurisdiction over individual citizens of Croatia or any other state. Under Article 6 and 7 the Tribunal's jurisdiction over national persons is limited by the Statute, and extends only to individuals accused of planning, instigating, ordering, committing, aiding or abetting a crime within the Tribunal's competence. Under the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence the Prosecutor has also asserted jurisdiction over individual witnesses. Rule 77, which the Prosecutor cites for support, allows the Trial Chamber to hold a witness who refuses or fails contumaciously to answer a question relevant to the issue before the Chamber in contempt and to fine that individual up to $10.000 or impose a term of imprisonment not exceeding 6 months. Persons who attempt to interfere with or intimidate witnesses may also be held if contempt. However, the Croatian government officials the Prosecutor seeks to sanction are not contumacious witnesses. The Prosecutor seeks to sanction those individuals because they are the government officials she assumes have custody and control of the documents she desires. She is not saying those individuals are seized of information based upon their own personal knowledge necessary for the prosecution at that time. Indeed, she has adduced no evidence they are either in possession of the documents she seeks or they have the authority to comply with her request or that they would be in a position to incur penalties under national law for doing so. She has arbitrarily identified them to serve essentially as hostages to force the Croatian Government to comply with her demand. Indeed, if sanctioning government officials in this manner is upheld as appropriate by the Tribunal it would de facto circumvent its well-understood lack of power to sanction states for non-compliance. Neither the Tribunal's Statutes nor Rules of Procedure and Evidence allow for such sanctions and the Tribunal should reject the Prosecutor's attempt to misuse those provisions in this case. Accordingly under the Tribunal's Statute and Rules of Procedure and Evidence it has no authority to direct a subpoena duces tecum to a state and no state or its officials may be sanctioned for failing to comply with such an order. The Tribunal should make it clear that it has no plans and indeed no authority to seek such a radical departure from the ordinary practice and procedure of international law and international tribunals. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can the state which has undertaken to cooperate with the Tribunal decline to comply with the process issued by the Tribunal just because it disputes the form of the process, that instead of being an order it is a subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why? It is a process, whether you call it a subpoena or you call it an order. As I understand, the states are under an obligation to comply with the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Respectfully, your Honour, we feel that a subpoena duces tecum issued to a sovereign state with a threat of sanction to its high officials is ultra vires for this Tribunal. We do not accept -- you call it order, we call it subpoena; let us just get on with it. We consider this a very fundamental, technical legal process, which is unacceptable and disallowed in the international context -- international law context. As I pointed out earlier, Croatia is complying and assisting with a request -- cooperating and assisting with a request for information. As the particular documents that are being requested are being requested with specificity, Croatia is at this very time cooperating and assisting. It may not seem important to some persons whether it is called an order or a subpoena, but in this area of international law it is creating the type of precedent that is ripe for misuse and misinterpretation in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So it is a question of form that you are disputing? It is basically the form that you are -- the form of the process that you are disputing?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Another question I want to ask: can a state refuse to provide a document -- can a state refuse to give a document to the Tribunal which has material bearing on a case just for the reason -- because it will infringe some state secret? Can it withhold material evidence on that ground?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and if the Tribunal feels that this is somehow rising to the level of failing to cooperate and assist, the Tribunal has the means available to it to go to the Security Council. In addition, I respectfully submit that the Tribunal at any time has the power to go to the Security Council and request this power. If the Security Council were to give this power to the Tribunal, we would not be here arguing. Our point is simply that today in this proceeding in these circumstances where we stand at the international practice of law it is ultra vires for this Tribunal to issue this tool of process against a sovereign state or to issue it against its individual high officials in their official capacity with a threat of sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Security Council has the power I think under Chapter 7 probably to take measures to restore international peace and order. While taking those measures, it must respect the sovereignty of the States involved, is a power of the Security Council in taking these measures, subject to the state sovereignties.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: The individual sovereign states have waived their claims for sovereignty in certain respects vis a vis the Security Council. Your Honour, we are not trying to argue that the Security Council is limited. What we are saying is that this Tribunal, which is a subsidiary organisation, does not have the same power vested in the Security Council. It does not prohibit this Tribunal from requesting such power through its founding body. It is only that such action has not been taken at this time and such power by this Tribunal does not currently exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This Tribunal is really a mirror of that Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The creation of this Tribunal Council is really a mirror of the Security Council. I got mixed up. This Tribunal is really a measure of the Security Council taken for the restoration of peace and national order.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, it is a measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So does it not have all the power the Security Council possesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I would respectfully submit that is a rather large leap and, by analogy, because one is empowered to engage in certain activities does not mean that you then immediately assume all the characteristics of the empowering institution. It actually would have been interesting had you said it is a mirror, but it is not. It is not a mirror of the Security Council, and it is only one measure, one manifestation of the exercise of the Security Council's power. The Security Council can do many things that this Tribunal is not empowered to do. This Tribunal has no police power, but the Security Council does. The Security Council has the authority to declare military action against an outlaw member state. Your Honour, I do not think anyone would believe that this Tribunal has the same power, but under the reasoning you have just proposed, if you have all the powers of the Security Council, you would have indeed all the powers which this Tribunal does not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I do not go to that extent, but all the powers necessary to make an effective institution, all the powers to make it an effective institution?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Perhaps, your Honour, this particular power is not necessarily -- is not necessary for the effectiveness. The power -- again we are very limited -- the power to issue a subpoena duces tecum against a state -- you have many other powers at your disposal. It is this one particular power and the extent of that power to high government officials with the threat of sanctions which we feel is ultra vires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do we have the power to compel the attendance of witnesses under Article 29?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Yes, but in that you also have to appeal to the cooperation and assistance of the member states, because you do not have a police power to go in and get those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So we would then issue a subpoena ad test -- help me we would issue that subpoena to the state to compel the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No. It is to individuals, witnesses, persons in their individual personal capacities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So we have the power under Article 29 to issue a subpoena ad testificatum to individual persons or witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Natural persons in their personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But not their official capacity?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: No, your Honour, because that is -- it is a back door method of trying to accomplish what is not available. It is a means of circumventing the inability to sanction the state. The only reason this high official would be -- if the only reason this high official is being sought to appear before the court is in his official capacity, then the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction over that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us suppose we assumed that an official in his official capacity was withholding documents because -- that his withholding of the documents constituted participation in the offence and that we therefore considered that he at the very least was a suspect. Would we not have the authority to issue an arrest warrant for such a party?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: For him as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Suspecting that he by withholding documents was aiding and abetting the commission of a crime?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Would you be asserting, your Honour, that he had a right to steal documents from a government, that he had the right to illegally take those documents from a government, because basically that is what is being proposed? If he is not allowed in his official capacity to give those documents over, is the Tribunal asking that he stale them and bring them to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, we have -- we are getting into the substantive offences, but in terms of command responsibility or even obedience to orders of superiors, if we concluded that such an individual by -- I just thought of this, so this may be rather --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: I am just thinking of my answer too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: -- not bizarre, but just thinking out loud, if we concluded that he, by obeying superior orders, that is the directions of the President, or whoever is the superior executive authority in the state -- that by obeying those orders and not complying with a subpoena, then he in a sense was aiding and abetting the commission of a crime, could we not, therefore, issue an arrest warrant for him as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that he has to be -- have aided and abetted in a crime of a different type, not a crime of a failure to produce documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No, I am not suggesting that. That is serious but that is not quite as serious as our substantive offences, but you could aid and abet before the commission or you could aid and abet --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: By now protecting in that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: If the Prosecutor truly felt that an individual in that circumstance in his personal capacity, even if he were trying to hide behind the cloak of government protection or state immunity, is indeed a suspect or someone subject to the criminal jurisdiction of this court, the Prosecutor should issue a subpoena --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: An arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: For that individual person. That is a different situation than what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be permitted to enlarge for one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is just a hypothetical thought just came into my mind. You will have an opportunity. Go ahead. Please. Finish up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARAGONA
utterances.text: Just there is not a restriction on the Prosecutor where she justifiably believes in good faith that this person would also qualify as a suspect under -- a suspect subject to the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, that she could not issue an arrest warrant or compel the appearance of that person. It does not mean that when that person appears that perhaps the same issues might not arise again, because then the burden would be on the Prosecutor to prove that it is in the individual's personal capacity not merely his position as a high official without personal knowledge that she is seeking to have this person before the Tribunal, but those are issues that would have to be looked at after the Prosecutor made a request for such a person to come forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Josipovic. Presentation by MR JOSIPOVIC.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I have not going to take too long. I am going to take advantage of such excellent translators and express myself in my own language. First of all, I think we have to establish with clarity that the purpose of today's hearing is not to establish which are the competencies that the Tribunal should have, but rather which it actually has according to the Statute and international law. The Prosecutor said a number of times that there was fear of inefficiency of the Tribunal and that the measures at the disposal of the prosecution and the Trial Chamber were not sufficient. He cited, in fact, that a subpoena was one of those measures that would be welcome to the Tribunal, and I believe that, but I allege that, unfortunately, or maybe fortunately -- it depends on the point of view -- the Tribunal does not have some competencies. It does not have them because such a measure has not been envisioned by the Statute of the Tribunal, nor by international law. It should be pointed out once again that the Republic of Croatia, like other states, has never for a moment called in question its duty to cooperate with the Tribunal and to carry out the Tribunal's orders. This is best testified to by the situation in which the Republic of Croatia, after the subpoena was suspended, and re-named into a request for cooperation or an order, did provide services to the Tribunal and started to supply the Tribunal with the documents requested of it. The question whether a subpoena should be issued or not is not merely a technical issue. In that case it would not be matter whether we call it an order, a subpoena, a warrant or a request. It is an extremely important question of international criminal law and I would be so bold as to say of the general world order. The road which could result in the prosecution and the Trial Chambers having at their disposal a measure called subpoena is a simple one. It simply needs to be introduced into international law, and the only proper way of doing that is for the Prosecution or the Tribunal to address the Security Council, and I am quite confident that if the Security Council considers it to be necessary for the efficiency of the Tribunal, it will introduce such a measure. The worst thing that could happen to this Tribunal, in my view, and to the development of international criminal law would be for a doubtful measure which is not rooted in the Statute, nor in the totality of practice so far of all known international courts to be introduced in the practice of international law somehow in an underhanded manner. As an argument that a subpoena does not exist against a sovereign state or high state officials, it was noted that there was no poena, no penalty, which are envisaged by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. If only that were the reason, then it would be easy to find a solution to it. The Tribunal would retreat; it would pass amendments to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; it would introduce such a measure and the problem would be resolved. But, of course, that is not possible. Just as my distinguished colleague and the Ambassador noted in his introductory statement, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence may only elaborate and provide in greater detail the basic principles contained in the Statute and international law. Instead of the Prosecutor suggesting to the Tribunal the only possible correct procedure to follow and that is addressing the Security Council and requesting competencies to issue subpoenas, the Prosecutor has chosen a different and less rewarding way. I can understand that -- it is very difficult to try to prove something that does not exist, and the Prosecutor in her detailed and extensive brief chose two methods, which should not be the rule in the future work of the Tribunal, and in the future practice of international criminal law. The first method is a method of a smoke screen. The Prosecutor presented a number of allegations, which are quite correct. By way of example, she spoke in detail about the formation and tasks of the Tribunal, about its rights to issue orders, about the duties of states to cooperate with the Tribunal, and the Republic of Croatian fully endorses those allegations of the Prosecutor. However, those unquestionable states are merely a smokescreen to conceal something that is legally unacceptable, probably in the hope that the Chamber or international public opinion -- and let us not question the fact that international public opinion is following this debate with great attention -- that by accepting the unquestionable assertions of the Prosecutor, it will also accept those that are doubtful and disputable and for which the Prosecutor has not provided a single valid argument. I should like to draw to the attention of the Chamber that the Prosecutor has not given a single example of any court of an international nature expressly mentioning a subpoena or using it either against the sovereign state or against an individual, a high official of that state, not one. A second method that the Prosecutor has used was incomplete or incorrect reference to certain sources, starting from the fact that the Appeals Chamber in the case of Tadic, which has nothing to do with the question of issuance of a subpoena, for example the competence, competence problem, or the interpretation of Article 3 of the Statute, without any firm logical connection was applied to the competence of the court to issue subpoenas. Furthermore, the Prosecutor referred to numerous provisions of national laws and probably underestimated those reading her brief, believing that perhaps nobody would verify these assertions. I will read for you only one, but I think a very eloquent example. The Prosecutor, among the numerous national legislations, also makes reference to German law, the Straf Prozess law -- Ordnung. She says in numerous provisions in paragraphs 48, 94-96 and 98 apparently they support the subpoena, but Article 96 reads: "Authorities and public figures may not be required to produce or to surrender files or other documents in their official custody if the supreme authority in their official agency declares that it would be detrimental to the welfare of the Federal Republic or a German state if the contents of such files or documents became known." I cannot understand that anybody could interpret this provision as supporting a subpoena against a state and its high officials. I would not like to repeat what has already been said by the previous speakers. I would like to underline, however, that the discussion on a subpoena is not a struggle of opinions amongst states with a common law system and those belonging to the system of continental Europe. That is a false dilemma. It is a struggle between two schools which have different views as to whether the Tribunal in performing its noble mission has any limits, whether the Statute and other norms are there merely to enable efficiency of the Tribunal, or are they there also to contain certain guarantee mechanisms not only in relation to the accused but also in relation to the global legal order? We firmly believe that that is the position of the Tribunal. We believe that the Tribunal does not have, nor does it want to have, unlimited competencies, nor does it want anyone sometime in the future to write about this Tribunal as one based on the Star Chamber. Certainly the assertions of the Prosecutor in favour of unequal treatment of states before this Tribunal for punishing individuals not according to explicit norms but by analogy, for the rules of the game to be changed after the match has already begun, and not to apply the generally accepted standards of international law and international criminal law such as nullem crimen nulla pene sine lege certainly do not fit into the view of the Tribunal as the international community expects to have of it. Clearly, and it would be unrealistic to expect this Tribunal not to have difficulties in the application of its competencies. There are diverse interests at stake and I appreciate that the positions of certain states may not always be in conformity with what this Tribunal could and should accomplish, but there are mechanisms to deal with that. His Excellency Simonovic and a number of amici curiae and our legal adviser stated very clearly that international law does have mechanisms at his disposal. These may be slow, but they are there, and they guarantee the future of this Tribunal. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I note your reference to -- the Prosecutor's reference to jurisdiction, to determine jurisdiction. I think that is a different proposition. I think then the question was whether or not the Trial Chamber and ultimately the Appeals Chamber had power to determine whether the Tribunal was legally established.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think that is true. I refer to the Germany Statute; does it not at least recognise the power to issue a subpoena to a state, albeit the power of a state or the right of a state to not comply because of its national interest; no?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: As I read it, the cited provisions of German law refer to what existed in all laws, and that is the right to determine -- to search the conditions for such procedures and the limits. There is certainly not a single punitive procedure in the world which would not envisage such a possibility. The only problem is in what way and whether this can be applied at all to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The reference to the need for effectiveness, that was where the Appeals Chamber was discussing its view of Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Extending it to international conflicts as well as internal, as it had been so limited in the past?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But are you saying that the Tribunal lacks the authority to issue an order that must be complied with?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You are simply saying that we may not -- the Tribunal may not exercise the penalty. Instead, we must report non-compliance to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: My position is that the Tribunal may issue orders, that states are duty bound to comply, but that the Tribunal does not have the possibility to determine the sanction itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is a determination, though, that a state has not complied with its obligation itself a sanction? . Does the Corfu Channel case not stand for that proposition and another case that was dealing with, I thought, a decision of the ICJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the position of this Tribunal with respect to the realisation of its goals is stronger than of the neighbouring court here regarding the Corfu Channel case. I think that this Tribunal may do something that is quite obvious, and that is to draw the attention of the Security Council to the fact that a state is not complying, and the Security Council has a broad range of measures from warnings to various types of sanctions that it may enforce against a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Mr Josopovic. Let us see. Mr Rivkin? Submission by MR RIVKIN

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it may please the court, it is our preference to go with our rebuttal argument last, of course, if that meets with your approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Are you saying that you have nothing to offer by way of direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Has everything been said and you wish to respond to the Prosecution's rebuttal. You may do that, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: We prefer to proceed with closing argument in rebuttal format, if your Honour does not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is acceptable except I think we can accomplish that today. The Prosecutor was correct when she said yesterday that it is Croatia that has challenged the subpoena and thus is really the moving party, but we are relaxing, I suppose, the rules. So you need not present it at this time. We will hear from -- I think we will hear from the remaining amici.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: We thank you your Honour. If I may just beg your indulgence for one second, I do not want to get it in the rebuttal argument, because I want to give a slight embellishment to the answer by my colleague to your hypothetical question. I think it is very important to realise as a matter of international law no official exercising his official duties in the conduct of which is otherwise perfectly appropriate can be sanctioned for it. I think the Nuremberg principle to which your Honour referred on a couple of occasions stands for the proposition on following orders and engaging in unlawful conduct is no defence, but it certainly would be, I would argue, a travesty of any international and domestic law to hold somebody whose actions are otherwise totally legitimate and proper -- to hold that person personally responsible under any theory, whether it be a contumacious witness or an aiding and abetting theory, which is very different from a situation where that individual, no matter what his government rank may be, was personally involved in aiding and abetting whether before or after the fact. I guess my point is that following and exercising ones legitimate duties per se cannot be a conduct that gives rise to any penalty, be it a conduct that occurred before or after an offence in issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we will hear now from -- thank you. Miss Vidovic, I have just -- I was just ready to proceed past you. I apologise. You may proceed and then we will hear from Miss Glumac. Presentation by MADAME VIDOVIC. MME VIDOVIC: Your Honours, Bosnia and Herzegovina in respect of the power of a judge or trial chamber of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a sovereign state and to its high government officials and apply appropriate remedies in the case of non-compliance with the subpoena takes the following stand. Based on provisions of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, it is not just a manifestation of the Security Council, as was quoted today, but it is an International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia established to try serious violations of the international humanitarian law. Based on the Statute of above all Article 18, paragraph 2, which says that in carrying out the investigation, the prosecution may, as appropriate, seek the assistance of the state authorities concerned, then Article 19, paragraph 2, which says that upon confirmation of an indictment, the judge may, at the request of the Prosecutor, issue such orders and warrants for the arrest, detention, surrender or transfer of persons and any other orders as may be required for the conduct of the trial. We do not see limitations as to the kinds of orders in the Statute of the Criminal Tribunal, and also in Article 29, paragraphs 1 and 2, which says that states shall cooperate with the International Criminal Tribunal, and also that states shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or order where, among other things, production of evidence is explicitly stated. We also think that the other provisions are fairly clear, and that the rules that provide enough competence of the Tribunal to communicate with other states as, for instance, Rule 39, 2, 3 and 4, which states that in the conduct of an investigation the Prosecutor may seek the assistance of any state authority concerned, and then the Rule 54, which says that, at the request of either party or in the first instance Trial Chamber, a judge or Trial Chamber may issue such orders that may be necessary for the purpose of an investigation or for the preparation or conduct of the trial. In other words, we believe that it is inherent to the Tribunal to decide which kinds of orders it will issue and not the state parties. In order to produce evidence and conduct the trial proceedings, a judge or a trial chamber of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia has the power to direct a request or subpoena to any government official regardless of his rank. As to avoid repetition, because I would state briefly that I accept all the arguments presented by the Prosecutor in respect of application of the international and criminal law, nonetheless, when Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, I am obliged to present certain facts that were only touched upon in yesterday's discussion. I am aware that the matters that we are discussing here today are just some theoretical issues regarding the power of a judge or the Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia to issue a subpoena, which non-compliance seeks appropriate remedies. I have to underline that both the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as Croatia are the states originating from the former Yugoslavia and the territorial jurisdiction of the International Criminal Tribunal extends to that territory. The whole issue that we are discussing here today are all bound exclusive to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, so both these states have a very specific role in relationship to the other sovereign states. As republics originating from the territory of the former Yugoslavia and in accordance with the Resolution 827 of the UN Security Council, are obliged to cooperate with the International Criminal Tribunal and other sovereign states. I am stressing here that the states originating from the former Yugoslavia, the newly formed states, are obliged to broadly cooperate with other sovereign states. They are also obliged in such a cooperation as signatories on the peace accord on Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is also known as the Dayton Peace Accord. Accordingly, all signatories of this agreement are obliged to full cooperation in investigation and prosecution of persons responsible for committing war crimes and other serious violations of international humanitarian law. Furthermore, since this is the cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal, it becomes clear that this cooperation has to be conducted based on rules by an international criminal tribunal and not any state legislation. Based on the Dayton agreements, they were obliged to adjust their legislations so that the full cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal would be made possible and Bosnia-Herzegovina complied with that. As far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, its obligation to fully cooperate with the International Criminal Tribunal is established even by the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, being the highest legal act of the state, namely according to Article 2, paragraph 8, of the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- not only is the state obliged to cooperate with the International Criminal Tribunal, but also with all its relevant authorities. I quote the relevant provision: "All relevant authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall cooperate and provide unrestricted access to evidence for the needs of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. They are particularly obliged to comply with orders issued in accordance with Article 29 of the Statute of the ICTY." Therefore, we consider that subpoenas duces tecum can be issued to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as any authority within Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e. to an official that represents that authority or with respect to its commitment to full cooperation. That does not just mean territory but for all the officials who are in certain positions in those respective governments. That means that the ICTY has the right to issue orders and subpoenas to other governments and other governmental bodies in order to conduct its investigations. Taking a stand that the judge or the Trial Chamber of ICTY has no power to issue a subpoena to sovereign states who are in possession of evidence relevant for the conducting of an investigation or a trial would mean that the Tribunal would not be able to accomplish the goal it was established for, that is to prosecute all persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. This would also mean that these states, especially the ones from the former Yugoslavia, which have been parties to the conflict in one measure or another -- if the state and its representatives are simply not willing to hand over such evidence, persons responsible for these violations would not be -- would never be brought to justice. This would be contrary to the idea expressed in the Resolution of the UN Security Council, for which the International Criminal Tribunal has been established, and which has been to a significant extent put at stake by the non-existence of a mechanism which would enable the Tribunal to bring the persons indicted to trial. I fully accept the Prosecutor's position in part 6 of the brief regarding the appropriate remedies to be taken by the International Criminal Tribunal in the case of non-compliance with subpoena duces tecum issued to such a sovereign state. When Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, and I stress its obligation full cooperation, I would add the following. If an actual person to whom the subpoena duces tecum was directed for some reasons that may not be justified does not appear before the Tribunal and the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia in exercise of its powers under Article 29.2 under the Statute of ICTY issues an appropriate order to the state authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina by which issuance the presence of the person directed is requested, then the state authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina are obliged to act under such order. Otherwise it would present a violation of its cooperation to cooperate with the Tribunal and to comply with its order and in that case the Tribunal would have the right to inform the Security Council about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You indicated that you are supporting the Prosecutor in part 6 of its brief, where it speaks to remedies, so I gather then it is your position that the Tribunal lacks the power to impose any penalties against a state for non-compliance with a subpoena. Is that your position? MME VIDOVIC: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: But that the Tribunal does have authority to impose -- issue a subpoena and impose a penalty against an individual in his official capacity if he fails to comply with a subpoena; is that correct? MME VIDOVIC: Yes, that is correct, to which I added -- I do not know if it was properly understood -- that the International Criminal Tribunal can request through its orders to fulfil its requests. In other words, if a state has an obligation to bring -- to produce a suspect if such a person is asked by the Tribunal through its order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So would then the Tribunal have to issue its order finding an individual in contempt and directing that individual to appear before the Tribunal to show cause why it should not be held in contempt; that order then should be sent to the state for its execution? MME VIDOVIC: No. That was not -- you did not understand me properly. I was talking about something else. It is about making sure that a person appears before the Tribunal. If there are political or other reasons for it not to do that, then there are measures against the state and the measures that you just mentioned, which means the contempt of court and then the rules from the Statute are applicable as cited by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Would the Tribunal have the authority to find a high governmental official -- whatever "high governmental official" means, but a governmental official -- in contempt and impose the penalty that is contained in our rules of a maximum of US$ 10.000 and/or six-month term of imprisonment? Would the Tribunal have the authority to impose that penalty against such an official if that official was not before the Tribunal, not present before the Tribunal? MME VIDOVIC: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And the Tribunal would not have to rely on the authorities of the state to execute such an order. MME VIDOVIC: In case a state does not fulfil -- answer to this order -- for instance, if it cannot objectively be done, as was the case here, or it does not want to, then the Tribunal should not rely on the authority of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We were informed that the Croatian Government has nominated a person for the purpose of cooperation of the Tribunal. Has the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina also done the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can you please tell us that authority for the purpose of the record? Perhaps I have not been able to make myself clear. MME VIDOVIC: Yes. I am the representative. I am Vasvija Vidovic, representative of the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Miss Vidovic. Mr Rivkin, are you available with us? Miss Glumac, how long will you need for your presentation?

utterances.speaker: MS. GRUMAC
utterances.text: I think a minute and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You may have two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRUMAC
utterances.text: I can do it from this place because I really do not need any paper: I will be very short. Your Honours, I should like to say after all that we have heard in the past two days that I fully see the arguments presented by the Croatian delegation, that is by the Croatian representatives, because in my opinion their arguments were thorough and detailed and well-founded. I would now like to refer only to what has been said by Mme Vidovic, because I think I really have nothing new to add regarding the subpoenas the possibility to issue subpoenas and all that, because I have already said in my brief that I think that the Tribunal does not have the right to issue a subpoena to a state or state officials. Therefore, as a comment to what has been said by Mme Vidovic, I would say in reference to what she said that in the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina there is a provision allowing the Tribunal to communicate directly with persons from which certain information or data is required, or to which any subpoena or order or any other request is addressed. I believe that that provision does not change in any way the status of the Tribunal in relation to that person, because I think there are no legal grounds for issuing a subpoena. The fact that such a provision exists in the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina can only give that country the right according to its own domestic law to sanction the person that it finds not to have complied with the order of the Tribunal. Therefore, whether this will be a sanction of a political nature, a penal sanction or not, I do not know, but I think that a subpoena addressed to such a person is not possible. Since non-compliance of a subpoena is not sanctioned in the Statute or the Rules of Procedure, therefore I think a subpoena cannot be sanctioned, or rather non-compliance with a subpoena cannot be sanctioned by this Tribunal, because, as has been stated repeatedly, and in particular yesterday by several amici yesterday, from Professors Pellet, Malanczuk, Zimmermann, Condorelli, who said that Rule 77 from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence cannot apply to people not complying with the subpoena. This is an institute that exclusively applies to witness non-compliance, and not non-compliance in the collection of evidence. I would also challenge the claims of the Prosecutor when she said that in the case of non-compliance with a subpoena it is possible to apply the provisions of Rule 19, that is to issue an arrest warrant, and this is something that I consider not to be correct, because in this case the person is called the accused. That is all I would have to say as a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In one of the briefs submitted by the amici curiae -- I do not remember which one -- the writer said that he had -- or she had -- reviewed the legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and had concluded that the President had the authority to direct ante Jelanic to comply with the subpoena. Did you see that amicus brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: I saw it but testimonies not according to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: It does not apply to the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the criminal law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as I know. I think that there we do not find that provision. There is no such criminal act of non-compliance with the orders of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think this amicus was speaking to the issue of whether or not Mr Jelanic has been instructed to appear -- provide the documents, by the proper authority. That amicus took the position that the proper authority had so instructed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Because you consider the proper authority to have been the Prime Minister; is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I will locate the brief and make you aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Because in that case we consider the Prime Minister not to be the person to give him orders where and when to appear, which we have already discussed, because I feel it is the duty of the Presidency of the Republic and not the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you very much. We will, when we return after our lunch break, hear from the amici, I think, Mr Ljubanovic. We will hear from you after -- when we return at 2.30 and then we will hear from Miss Wedgwood and that will conclude then the submissions of the amici and then we will hear from the Prosecutor. So we will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.10pm) (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will now hear from Mr Ljubanovic, please. Presentation by MR LJUBANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LJUBANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. I am ready and willing to answer any questions that you may have, but I would like to ask you to allow me to say a few more words about something that is not contained in our amicus curiae brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You have been with us for two days now and so I believe that you deserve some special allowances, so you may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LJUBANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday's statements by the amicus curiae showed that with respect to certain important issues having to do with the application of the institutes of subpoena duces tecum in relation to states and state officials, there appears virtually to be a consensus. It was thus noted that there are no sanctions on the part of the Tribunal towards a state for non-compliance with a subpoena duces tecum. This was a position that was accepted by the distinguished Prosecutor. I would add that if there is no penalty, there is no subpoena, because subpoena means "under penalty", and without a penalty, that is an empty threat, as His Honour has noted; then what remains, what we find in the UN Resolution 827 and in Article 29.2 of the Statute, which says that states are obliged to comply with all requests for cooperation and orders of the Tribunal, but such unity of view was not achieved with respect to the possibility of issuing a subpoena duces tecum towards state officials and individuals and with respect to the sanctioning of those officials for not complying with the subpoena. But a number of the amici curiae did take stands which are of significance for this question. Thus, for instance, it was noted that a state official was a state agent, who upholds the position of the state, otherwise he would not be a state agent. Furthermore, that Rule 77(A) applies to witnesses. A witness who refuses to answer questions by the Chamber and is thus in contempt of court. Also, as stated by Mr Zimmermann, for instance, the state is entitled to protect its state and national interests, and, as the distinguished President of the Trial Chamber pointed out, the Tribunal has no interest in violating national interests. Finally, it was noted that not in a single legal act, statute or in international law in general is any penalty envisaged if a state official fails to hand in a document, which means that sanctioning such a person would be an offence of the principle of nullem crimen nullem pena. If we were to add to what was stated yesterday that Article 29, paragraph 2, speaks about the cooperation of states and their obligation towards the Tribunal and not of state officials, then the Republic of Croatia in its constitutional law on cooperation of Croatia with the International Tribunal has designated that the Government of the Republic of Croatia is the main body for cooperation with the Tribunal. If we add that according to the jurisdictions of continental Europe, tribunals cannot forcefully request documents from the state or state officials; namely they can request it but these may not comply if state interest is at stake. Mr Josipovic read a provision from the German Strafa Prozess Ordnung, and I must say there was a similar provision in Article 102 of the Penal Code of Croatia. An interesting viewpoint was voiced yesterday by Mr Pellet, namely that the Tribunal cannot equate the state and the state official with a person, that it cannot address a minister, that is a state official, but that it may call on him as an individual. This appears to me to be very complicated. In my view such a person may be invited as an individual only if a statement is required on relevant facts which are not related to his ministerial functions. Otherwise, it is impossible to separate such a person from his duties of Minister which he is performing. Finally, I do not know whether from the brief of the amicus curiae the message is clear, the message which the Croatian Association of Criminal Science and Practice which I represent here wishes to convey. This Association has close to 700 lawyers in its membership engaging in criminal law either as judges, public prosecutors, defence counsels or university professors. Therefore, I do not know whether this message, this idea which we wish to convey to you is clear from this document, but I will, therefore, say now it is an old idea that a criminal code applies to criminals only and the law on criminal procedure does not take into account the people that are being accused. This speaks to the complexity of legal procedure, of penal procedure. The substance of any penal procedure is to strike a balance between the demands for effectiveness of the penal procedure and the protection of the personal rights of the accused and the rights of the defence. Because the accused may be innocent. However, the procedure before an International Tribunal is even more complicated, because a balance has to be found between the effectiveness of the procedure and measures limiting the rights of sovereign states. If the International Tribunal feels that the proceedings are not effective enough, and that, according to the existing provisions of the Statute and the Rules and international law in general, it does not have at its disposal the necessary body of measures for more effective jurisdiction, and this is a problem that was referred to by the distinguished Prosecutor, and I understood her very well, the crucial issue is not of the subpoena because of the penalty, but because of the effectiveness of the proceedings. If that is so, then this very difficult and complicated problem of finding additional measures further to restrict the rights of sovereign states, even subpoena duces tecum, should not be resolved by the Tribunal itself but by the Security Council of the United Nations, but not in the way that was suggested here, that frequently, every week or every month, as Judge McDonald noted, the Trial Chamber should run to the Security Council, but rather that the Council should find a system -- define a system of new measures for the greater effectiveness of the International Tribunal. I fear that an order of the Tribunal to issue a subpoena duces tecum to states and state officials in a situation when, to use a mild term, there are numerous dilemmas, and yesterday's discussion by distinguished, world-renowned law professors showed that this was so, would even further complicate relations between the state and the International Tribunal, and would not contribute to the greater effectiveness of the International Criminal Tribunal, which is the ultimate goal and meaning of these debates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you believe that the Rules that the Tribunal has adopted, Rules 11, 59 and 61, that provide that the President may report to the Security Council non-compliance -- do you believe that those are valid Rules enacted with the authority founded in the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. LJUBANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. I think they are valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is that not a penalty of sorts?

utterances.speaker: MR. LJUBANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, as far as I have been able to gather from the debate this past two days, it appears that the proceedings before the Tribunal are not effective enough, and that the solution is to be found in the Statute and the Rules. Certainly the Statute could not deal with all issues and especially those having to do with the procedure of the court itself. Then the Tribunal was authorised to fill in those gaps with the Rules on Procedure and Evidence, but in spite of those provisions, and one of those is the one you are referring to, this to me seems -- it does not seem to me that there is no possibility for even greater effectiveness. Therefore, I think that we should not try to stretch interpretations of existing Rules, but, rather, that we should not -- that the provisions that exist -- that the core of measures that exist are not satisfactory and that the Security Council which, as we have already said, has broad-based possibilities of action should take steps to make those proceedings more effective. When I refer to effectiveness, I am implying guarantees that the perpetrator of a crime does not go unpunished, because only then is a trial proceedings effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What I am asking you and what I am suggesting is that from what I understand, from listening to many persons for the last day and a half or so, the word "subpoena" is a term that is unknown in civil law systems, and that at least in common law systems where it is used, or at least in some common law systems, that term is construed in a way so as to provide that it would follow automatically if there is non-compliance with a subpoena, there would follow a criminal and/or -- a criminal penalty and/or a fine. In drafting our Rules of Procedure and Evidence -- as you know, we have both civil and common law judges -- and we came together and we have drafted something that we are very proud of, but they combine civil and common law concepts. So what I am suggesting is that perhaps the term "subpoena", which carries with it a very particular meaning in some common law systems, could be used in our procedures without carrying it to the full extent of those known and acceptable common law penalties and/or fines, and that, if reporting to the Security Council is a penalty, and cases have been cited in the briefs that we have received that say that other judicial institutions -- just noting non-failure to cooperate, I suppose, is a penalty in itself -- that that would perhaps solve the concern that I hear from some of the speakers. That is they say you cannot impose a fine, or you cannot imprison on a state, and that is the natural and only understanding of the word "subpoena." What I am suggesting that that need not be the only understanding, that we as a Tribunal, combining civil and common law concepts, may devise. So if we have the authority to report to the Security Council and if states have an obligation to comply with orders because of their obligation under the UN Charter, and under international law, then it seems to me that there needs to be an education process about this term "subpoena", then rather than being so offended by it and assuming that it calls for a certain response, because that is how it has been used typically, that that need not be the only approach. So if a subpoena was issued, calling it a subpoena, but if it was understood that the penalty as it relates to states would be at least in part what we have already done in three different rules, what is the problem as it relates to states?

utterances.speaker: MR. LJUBANOVIC
utterances.text: It is questionable whether one can sanction a state or not. It is the unanimous view that a penalty cannot be imposed on a state. If, as Professor Condorelli said, the only sanction is to notify the Security Council, and thus denounce this non-compliance -- if the Tribunal is satisfied with that, then the problem is not so great, but if the desire is for the Tribunal itself to be able to take such measures of punishment because for the present in the Rules there is no such possibility -- sanctions can only be enforced against a witness who has come and refuses to testify. But one might turn the thing around and say: "Why need we use the term 'subpoena' when, according to Article 29, paragraph 2, the Tribunal may issue an order which are also obliges the state to satisfy?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If a subpoena were issued to an individual and included in the subpoena was a statement or notification that failure to comply with this subpoena may result in a fine not exceeding 10,000 US dollars and/or imprisonment for a term not to exceed six months, would that solve the nullem crimen problem you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUBJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that applies to individuals only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As it is implicit in my question. Actually, I will make it two questions. First, as to individuals in their personal capacity, and then as to individuals in their official capacity. As to individuals, period, in terms of them being put on notice that this is unlawful, failure to comply, this is unlawful; would that solve that problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. LJUBANOVIC
utterances.text: In the case of individuals, I think that there are no problems, and a subpoena, since it is envisaged in the Rules by the 1995 amendment, it can be issued and that individual is obliged to comply to the summons and come as a witness, because the subpoena, as I understand it, means that he must come to testify bringing documents with him. If he does not come, then he can be punished, and that is quite in order according to the rules, but in the case of a state official; difficulties arise because, according to domestic law, a state official is entitled to withhold delivery of documents, if that is in the state interest or in the general interest. I will tell you what the provision as according to the Croatian law are at present. According to Croatian law, a court may issue orders to an individual, including state officials and state bodies, to deliver certain documents, but there is a specific provision saying this a state official and a state body may withhold delivery of documents if that is in the general interest, and, according to our law, the Trial Chamber passes the determination. Then that state body in a general way, not directly, conveys to the Trial Chamber this general interest. If the Trial Chamber insists, there is no forcible execution of the order; that is, the document cannot be taken away, but the whole issue has to be raised to a higher level. Therefore, a solution may be found in this case too, not for the state to deliver the documents to the Trial Chamber and then for the Trial Chamber to assess whether a national interest is at stake or not, because in all probability it is the state that knows best what its own interests are, but that state might convey indirectly to the Trial Chamber that state interest is involved, and then I would accept the proposal that has already been made that if that Chamber feels that such non-compliance is unwarranted, then it could report it to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have no additional questions. Thank you very much for submitting your brief and thank you for coming and responding to our questions and giving your comments. We have one more amicus, Miss Wedgwood. Presentation by MISS WEDGWOOD

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You too have been here for a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: It is a pleasure to be here your Honour. If only for gathering good teaching materials, this has been an extremely interesting hearing for me. I thought if I might address where I think the conversation has gotten to, because it has changed a bit, I think, since the beginning of the hearing. I will do so very briefly and do please stop me when I have used up my time.
