I do think the starting point is in this kind of a case which addresses command responsibility there is a unique need for the kinds of records that only a government will have. The military records, though sensitive, are, if you like, the res gestae, the speech acts that oftentimes constitute command responsibility, either the orders that are given, even the orders that are not given, the reports that did or did not go to the commander. So this is not simply third party records by an interested bystander. These are the very gravamen of the offences in issue. Unlike a proceeding between states, where you can deal with questions of privilege by penalising the state by forcing them to concede a point or have an adverse inference drawn against them, here the liberty or incarceration of an individual is at stake, so you cannot really -- there is a kind of a mismatch between the people who control the evidence and the parties whose most sensitive interest and liberty is at issue. Much of the conversation has seemed to concern worries about overbreadth or materiality or national security problems, and those I take it really are all put to one side, because here the issue before us is the principle in se of whether there can be a command given to a sovereign country to turn over records, and whether there should be a motion to quash on grounds of overbreadth or laches or some kind of framework for protecting sensitive secrets that affect a country's future security interests are different issues entirely. I think your Honour is correct, if I took the drift of your questions properly, that the court is ultimately forced to proceed on the principle of effectiveness, which has been recognised by many tribunals -- the ICJ, for example, in a certain expenses case where Judge Percy Spender said: "If two interpretations of a document are possible, that which is favourable to the accomplishment of the purpose and not restrictive of it must be preferred"; and in the ICJ case, the headquarters agreement dispute, Judge Shahabadin said that: "Certainly the court should always take care to satisfy itself of its authority to act, but it is equally appropriate to be mindful of the risk of wishing to be so very certain of its powers as to discover overly refined reasons for not exercising those which it may fairly be thought to have." A complicated sentence but a simple idea, that where you are dealing with the growth of an institution, where it is impossible for a legislative body to specify in advance every permutation of facts that may come upon the body, inevitably the institution is forced to look to its own nature, the teleological principle that international lawyers like to talk about that you have to look at what is essential to the accomplishment of the institution's very purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you have a citation to that last quote or is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Judge Shahabadin was -- I do not think it is in my brief, your Honour, I apologise. 1988, ICJ at page 63 and the Percy Spender from the certain expenses was 1962, ICJ, at 186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do not draw any conclusions from the questions that I may ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I have learned not to do that in court, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I act as devil's advocate sometimes. You know if you argue before court, sometimes the questions they are asking you is because they agree, disagree or just need clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I only mention your Honour's questions to say they did make reference to this principle of effectiveness which has been recognised by the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It has a lot. Particularly in one of the briefs, and we did not hear from that amicus -- Professor Salcedo, I think. He submitted a brief that really focuses on that. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I do think one thing I might add to the conversation is just to point out that the source of authority here that undergirds the Tribunal's power -- it is not simply the Chapter 7 authority of the UN Charter straight up, but as well the Dayton Agreement, which was an agreement among three belligerents, and there is nothing wrong with being a belligerent. There is not a question of the justness of the war. What is before this Tribunal in its competence is how the war was fought. It is the lawfulness and tactics of the war but not why the war was fought. There were three belligerents, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and each of them were parties to the Dayton Agreement, and under Dayton each of them agreed to comply with the orders of the Tribunal, to cooperate with the Tribunal and great benefits were gained by each of these three parties under Dayton: the intervention of the international community, by the commitment of armed forces, arms control agreements, a great many things, in exchange -- not in exchange -- alongside of this promise to cooperate. One need not found the Tribunal's authority here solely on the question of Chapter 7 in se and the Tribunal's Statute in se, but as well on the promise of the parties to cooperate and, if you like, essentially a waiver of any claim of immunity or sovereignty that they might otherwise have. I take it it is conceded by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Before you proceed, if you do not mind, from that point, you mentioned that in your brief, the Dayton Accords. My question is: I think one of the amici -- or it may have been Croatia -- said that really nothing was added by the Dayton Accords, no specificity. I think it was Mr Malanczuk, maybe. Nothing specific was added to the obligation from the Dayton Accords, and my question is: is it just a reaffirmation of the duty to cooperate, and if there were no Dayton accords, would not all member states have the same obligations? So if the Dayton Accords gives a greater obligation, what is it? Of course it is a treaty. In your brief you say here there is at least a treaty-based relinquishment of sovereignty, but do you really need it, and, if so, what does it give this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: As I believe Croatia itself has said Chapter 7 authority under the UN authority is a kind of Protean power, a plenary power but there are, to be fair, debates about its extent, its outer limit. There are, as any denizen of the UN hallways knows, debates about the appropriate balance of authority between the General Assembly and the Security. Proposals for expanding the Security Council are based upon the concern that some countries have about the intervention of the Council into civil wars and civil conflicts. So I do think that Dayton, if you like, gives you a comfort factor, that it gives you a second stanchion upon which to build. One does not have to address in a wholly abstract way the outer limits of Chapter 7 authority, because the signature of the parties at Dayton gives you have a separate voluntary consensual basis for their cooperation with the Tribunal. So I think Chapter 7 alone here would be fully sufficient, in my own view, especially since this concerns the belligerence in the territory of Yugoslavia, but I do think their signature on the dotted line at Dayton gives you a second pillar upon which to allay any concern among any of the members of the United Nations that this implicates Chapter 7 authority alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you join the Prosecutor then in its use of the term "coercive" as to states of the former Yugoslavia but "mandatory" as to all states, or if you do not join in that term, do you consider there is of a different obligation for those states that are in the former Yugoslavia, a position that Croatia disagrees with very strongly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I guess my own common law background would probably show your Honour in generally declining to reach questions one does not have to. I am not sure I would adopt a phrase of culprit states because I am not sure that is pertinent here. I do think again it is their status as belligerents in the war, the conduct of their officials, their soldiers, their paramilitary, their citizens, is what is in issue for the Tribunal. In that sense they present a distinct category of state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: There may be some other states, though, who have that same type of information. That is perhaps states that participated with UNPROFOR. They may not have been belligerents, but they still being on the scene, so to speak, also may have possession of that type of information. Would the same duty that you suggests belongs to belligerent states belong to them?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: A harder question, your Honour, for a couple of different reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is not before us, I realise.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Indeed. The United Nations has always been very sensitive about its status as an international organisation. For example, on the Geneva Conventions their peace-keeping troops always operate according to the Geneva Conventions and yet the UN is quite dainty about insisting that it is not itself a party to the Geneva Conventions. I do think the case before us is the easiest one, because not only were the belligerents there, not only is the Russianae locus, Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia itself, but the very records in question one presumes are still in the former Yugoslavia. Whether a national contingent that contributed to UNPROFOR or IFOR or SFOR with records that may not be in the former Yugoslavia would be obliged to turn those over -- I am sure those countries would want to cooperate with the Tribunal. I guess my instinct is not to try to sketch every possibility before one has to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In your brief you say that Herceg-Bosna has never been a state and if it was a state is no longer a state. Are you going to speak to that? It seems it is related to what we are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I was surprised this had not arisen in any of the other briefing materials. Herceg-Bosna was, if you like, an attempt by the Croatian community in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina to create some kind of autonomy for itself, rather like the rump Republic of Srpska, which had no legal status before Dayton. Herceg-Bosna has never been recognised, has never gained any juridical status in the eyes of anyone except is own denizens and, I believe, the Republic of Croatia. It is certainly a non-entity since the conclusion of the 1994 federation agreement on March 19th 1994, which created this Muslim/Croat federation which now has become the federation of the Dayton Accord. Since Dayton itself it is clear that Bosnia and Herzegovina is only made up of the Republic of Srpska and the federation. Herceg-Bosna has no status. Thirdly, the Croatian member of the Bosnian national Presidency, Mr Zubac, has now declared, the entity, community, republic whatever you like to call it of Herceg-Bosna is no more, so even if there had been a claim, that is now defunct. Here you have of a question that the records in question are not a sovereign entity. It is as if they are the records of a private company happened to wind up in the state archives of France or Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia. What I fear might distinguish me as going back to American criminal law, there used to be a distinction drawn between the act of production and the records in themselves. There were debates about giving immunity for the act of production as opposed to whether the records themselves were private in some way. The old Omstead case from the turn of the century, a right of privacy in records in themselves. Here when a claim is made of national immunity or national sovereignty or sovereign immunity, what is really being spoken of, I think, is not simply the act of production but whether there is kind of a national work product, if you like, that these are governmental records that belong and are private to the sovereign. Here that is clearly not the case. These were the records of an association, Herceg-Bosna, which has never gained international status as a sovereign so I think the analogy here is not to what the records of Croatia or Bosnia itself might be but the records of a labour union, private company or community association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Of course then the right -- the national security interest, there would be none. There might be a claim there once again that the subpoena should not lie against a high governmental official in his official; capacity, or would -- that issue would still have to be resolved, would it not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: On the national security claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Not the national security claim. I understand that that would go out the window according to your--

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Every country has a fair worry about its future security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As to these documents, what you are saying is they are documents that belong to Herceg-Bosna, and they do not belong to Croatia -- they belong to Herceg-Bosna, so any claim to national security would be unsuccessful. Still Croatia might very well assert the proposition that a subpoena should not lie against a state or a state official acting in his official capacity. This state official, now, is acting in his official capacity as the custodian of these records which, using your approach, could not in any way endanger their national security, since they do not relate to their security seemingly, but could they not raise that first claim, no subpoena against an individual in his official capacity?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: The issue of the proper addressee of a subpoena still exists. I readily concede that but I do think in terms of both how the Tribunal feels about its own efficacy, what it is fair to infer about its own power, the fact that the records being sought do not lie at the core, if you like, of sovereignty but are just a matter of a custodian of convenience goes to what is a kind of prudent inference that the Tribunal would want to draw about its own powers. If I might mention one thing about which I fear comes from my own vantage point in New York where I probably spend too much time watching the Security Council close up, but when one thinks about what kind of sanctioning scheme is fair to infer within the power of the Tribunal, and Croatia itself concede that these orders can being made compulsory, they are mandatory orders, they just raise the question of how to enforce them, the Security Council has become a very busy place. Where formally they might have met eight hours a day, they now meet dozens of hours a week. Their denizens never go home. So the kind of functional judgement one would draw about the ability of the Security Council to hold hearings on the scope of subpoenas, the proper addressees of subpoenas, if one is construing what would have been the Council's intention, do they mean themselves to be the appellate body from the Tribunal for the enforcement of subpoenas? Given their workload with Zaire, Albania and a host of other problems, it just seems very implausible they would have drafted a statute for this Tribunal that would have tended to make them a councillor of constant resort for the enforcement of orders or subpoenae that these Tribunal might issue. If I might also just mention, I do think there is and analogy that has not been drawn one on having the Tribunal itself issue sanctions. One is that in Rule 61(D), which I do not think has been disputed here, third party states can be ordered by the Tribunal to freeze the assets et cetera of departments who fail to surrender. So the Tribunal is not only put to resort to the Security Council but acts itself under Rule 61(D) to enforce its orders of arrest. Second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is mentioned in the Statute itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: There is clear -- there is explicit authority for that notion, I do believe; if I am not, correct. I am not talking about 61(D) now. I am talking about another provision in the Statute that I do not look at often but I will find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This clause chiefly relates to the accused, not to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: No, it is a defendant who fails to surrender; correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not a witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: If I misspoke I apologise. A person who fails to yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The accused would be one who has been indicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: My point is -- the question of what analogy you would draw, the argument has been made that heretofore the Tribunal has only spoken of going to the Security Council to give teeth to its orders and therefore one should not infer any other option in the case of subpoenae to witnesses. In 61(D) there is an exception to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is mentioned in the Statute in -- in the penalty section in Article 24 in the penalties Section 3: "In addition to imprisonment, the Trial Chambers may order the return of any property and proceeds acquired by criminal conduct including by means of duress to their rightful owners, so that 61(D) was an attempt to provide for a rule to give effect to that specific penalty, I think, in the Statute, but that certainly, though, is also authority for the proposition that the Trial Chamber deals with third states, of course, who are obviously not parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I might also take it, your Honour, although it might be a provisional measure which will allow the preservation of assets for their later return to anybody who was wrongfully deprived of them, it has a course of effect on the defendant. He cannot go to Switzerland and live off his bank account out of reach of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will try to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I would also draw a different inference from the Maastricht Treaty, the European Court of Justice Treaty, than some of the other amici have. The fact that the ECJ as amended by Maastricht does allow a fine on non-compliant states shows that it is not outside the range of magistrates to have an International Tribunal act directly on states in the course of fashion. Although there it was done by explicit treaty provision, I do think the fact that it was accepted by the European Community -- the Union -- shows that this is within the range of -- the repertory of remedies that one could conceive of for a Tribunal, and therefore to find it be within a Tribunal's inherent authority is not so peculiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Zimmermann spoke to that. What he said, if I recall it correctly, is that that treaty represented as significant a waiver of sovereign immunity as does the waiver under Chapter 7, which is a very extraordinary statement. Of course he is not here to tell me I am wrong. That is how I recall what he said. He said: and even under that circumstance it had to be amended to provide for a penalty to be imposed. The problem is that it is the Security Council that is empowered to devise enforcement measures. So it is really a little different situation, I think, than a treaty. Then they devise the enforcement measures, in this instance the Tribunal, then they give us explicit power. Then they say that we are to carry out our judicial functions, or at least the Secretary General says that we are to carry out our judicial functions without political considerations, and they tell us to draft rules to get the job done. I think that is a little bit different than the EC treaty but anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I do not mean to belabour the analogy, your Honour but clearly the European Union is deepening and it is a very gemutlich community of states but it shows this is not an un-thought-of kind of remedy for a Tribunal to have. Whether one infers it here or not it a different question. Finally, let me just say, in general listening to the arguments -- and it has been very interesting for me because I do think that common law lawyers and civilian lawyers at times do have different ways of approaching problems. Common law lawyers probably tend to be more functionalist and make arguments from prudence and inference -- for prudence and function, more than civilians who prefer texts, the mentality of codification, but I do think here at times the search for explicit authority for what the Tribunal might do in relation to the enforcement of the subpoenae or the orders was confusing levels of authority, if you like. I mean, five quite distinct questions: is it within Chapter 7 authority of the Security Council? Did the Security Council delegate it to the Tribunal as a potential power to draw upon? Is it within the rules that the Tribunal has yet created? Is it within the rules that the Tribunal could create, because I note under Rule 6 that the Tribunal can draft a new rule with immediate efficacy, and if it is concerning something that is prospective one might have to reissue an order, if you like, but if it is prospective and there is no problem of nulle pene sine lege, a new Rule creating a coercive measure to enforce orders of document production might take effect immediately. Finally, the fifth, if you like, is what authority the court might find without a formal rule tailored to a case, and if you can forgive me for drawing an American analogy, in the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure and Evidence there is always a housekeeping rule at the end that says if there is something not provided for the court can use its discretion to craft a rule for the particular case. Here even if it is not deemed to be part of the existing authority of rules, the court might well -- the hand-tailored case, the bespoke suit, it is often within the compass of a court to devise a procedure or a rule for a particular case that has not yet come up. I think that some of the concern, for example, about rule 77 -- was contempt provided for in 77 this exact set of facts? -- is really beside the point, because the court could either craft a new rule or could find it within its inherent authority even if not explicitly provided for in 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If we were then to determine that failure to comply with a subpoena by an individual or state could result in a penalty, the fact that 77 does not provide for a penalty under those circumstances -- does not provide for those explicitly -- would not violate the nullem crimen principle?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: In so far as one is dealing with a prospective duty to produce documents likened to civil contempt, not criminal contempt, a question of money or incarceration, whose only purpose is coercive and which is relieved as soon as production is made, if that were prospective, then there is no problem of ex post facto or nullem -- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ex post facto. I like that better. I am more used to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I can never do the Latin quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You mentioned Rule 6 in terms of the amendments and it could apply immediately. That is true. Rule 6 provides: "An amendment shall enter into force immediately but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or the suspect", as we amended it in April, I think, "in any pending case." "An accused or a suspect in any pending case": that sounds like it is time for us to amend that Rule too, if we decide to deal with contemptors, so if we were then to find that we could issue subpoenas to individuals and if a penalty could be imposed upon that individual who fails to comply similar to what is already provided in Rule 77, would that violate the ex post facto rules -- principles, since it is not presently in force? The second question is: the Prosecutor takes the position that if you put in that notice your failure to comply or order or subpoena -- it will be an order really to show cause -- put in that -- I guess it would have to go on the subpoena in the first instance -- if you put that in there saying your failure to comply will result -- could result -- or will result in these penalties, that would obviate that problem. What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Actual notice whether it is in parking tickets or in subpoenas is always a good prophylactic act for due process. Whether one would want to formally withdraw the subpoena and reissue the order or simply deem the subpoena to be a continuing order of production with new rule that future failure to comply would be penalised or coerced in the following way, it would certainly relieve any problem of ex post facto. Finally let me just mention one last thing, your Honour, and I beg the indulgence of the court for taking too much time. I do think in real life in the chaos of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia that the question of to whom one can address the subpoena, in particular whether you can name an individual person as the addressee of the subpoena, is crucially important. As one saw in the events of the subpoena addressed to Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the Defence Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina apparently ignored the instructions of his own Government, where the formal authority -- the organisation charts of governments do not work the way they are supposed to on paper, and where political authority is quite uncertain, where there are, in fact, still recalcitrant communities and parties, the ability to address a subpoena to a particular individual who has actual custody is very important to the efficacy of the Tribunal, and so too for the sake of the probativeness of the fact-finding, you want somebody who knows how the records were kept, whether they are complete, whether they were authentic. All the suppositions of administrative regularity, bureaucratic regularity, that often in common law systems allows an exception of the hearsay rule that allows any old custodian to bring them in. In the case of a civil conflict or an international conflict, there is a peculiarly cogent need for custodians and producers who know whereof they speak and are not simply custodians of convenience to make sure that the records are what they purport to be and are complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you think it might not be better, if you wanted to achieve that, to address the subpoena to the state and direct the state to designate that official who is the custodian and who has the best information regarding the contents of -- contents and locations of these documents? Then you avoid this problem of "I am not the custodian", that kind of? Business. Then you put the burden right on the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: If the state were the party, that would be a great thing to do your Honour, but since it is the liberty of an individual that is at stake here, I think for the sake of the probativeness of the fact-finding which is again crucial through a criminal trial, one cannot delegate that choice necessarily to the state. The Prosecutor has a good faith duty to seek the best possible proof. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Or perhaps designate a named individual or in the alternative a person with the most knowledge. I do not know. Maybe because I think we have had, Miss Glumac, how many, five hearings on this point, trying to resolve this whole question. In my own mind I am trying to decide how we might make it clearer who is to come but I hear what you say. Do you have anything else because I have some questions from what you have raised in your brief?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now you find in your brief that the Tribunal has the authority to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a state and to high governmental officials. You also find that we could hold the state and the individual in contempt. If we are to hold the individual in contempt, need that individual be before the Tribunal, before we could make such a finding, and if he or she is not here, would that be a trial in absentia?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I do not believe so, your Honour. The individual need not be present. Here one can make a direct analogy to Rule 77. The contempt power to -- in the case of an individual who has failed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Answer or interfere.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Let me think for a moment. Certainly the contempt power extends to conduct that occurs outside the presence of the court because the interference or intimidation might well have occurred in a different country. In so far as the sanction is designed to simply be coercive, is analogous to a civil contempt, relieved the instant that obedience is shown, that kind of a civil penalty does not require personal presence. If it was criminal contempt, I guess there is an argument that, like any other criminal penalty, since the Tribunal does not have in absentia authority to try defendants in absentia that even criminal contemnors should not be tried for criminal contempt before they are brought before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In the US Federal Rules of Procedure it is specifically provided for in criminal contempt.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Crawford takes the position -- the Prosecutor takes the position that the Tribunal lacks the power to issue subpoenas to states because -- well, for a number of reasons, I suppose, but one reason is -- excuse me; I am sorry -- to penalise a state, because Article 6 and 7.1 really puts the focus on individuals. I am not stating his argument as eloquently as he did. Where do we get this power to penalise states, assuming we have the power to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a state, and is the fact that -- is Article 6 -- does Article 6 -- do Article 6 and 7.1 somehow limit our authority to penalise individuals?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: If I can just a moment to turn to Article 6 and 7.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You really were the last person, Miss Wedgwood. We will be recessing soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I take 6 and 7, your Honour, simply to be, if you like, a restatement of the general rule or at least the practice of criminal law, international law, that heretofore states have not been deemed to be appropriate parties for criminal liability. Again there is some changing mood on this. The principles of state responsibility that are presently before the International Law Commission speak of the possibility of states being criminal actors, but I take 6 and simply to be a question of who is the appropriate target. Who is the appropriate class of defendants for the Tribunal to address as the indictees of charges. I share Mr Crawford's, I suppose, delicacy that if it is all in a word -- if calling it a binding order instead of a subpoena will make a happy marriage of the parties, then there is every reason to recast a request for an order in a way that will lead to amity and compliance but I do not share his diffidence on the penalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Can you do that if you are going to issue a subpoena to an individual in his official capacity and then have a document entitled subpoena duces tecum to an individual and then have also a document called an order to the state? What the Prosecutor has done in the two instances is in one subpoena address it to the state and then the second addressee on the same coversheet is the individual. So in a sense, I mean, you are going to have to decide what you want to do, unless you separate the documents, and name one an order to the state and then a subpoena duces tecum to an individual, or is that not a problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: It seems to be a bit of nominalism what you call it. If it is a compelling order, the coercive effect, the legal obligation to comply is the same. The question of penalty can be put ahead to a forward step so whether you call it a subpoena or call it a compulsory order or order to produce, mandatory order to produce, it is all -- again for the sake of -- the mission -- the burden of the Tribunal to craft a cosmopolitan criminal procedure that plays well in the sensibilities of both civil and common law lawyers -- I might choose the more ecumenical term, but I do not think what word is used really goes to the power of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We do not have -- an argument is made that we do not have a Rule at this time dealing with contempt for failure to comply with the production of documents. Now that is starting to sound like a good way to put it, a subpoena. Would we need a Rule on that? We talked a little bit about that a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I have heard the argument. Perhaps I am too much of a latitudinarian but as at Rule 77(A), a witness that refuses to answer a question relevant to an issue before the Tribunal or fails contumaciously to answer a question -- if you like, an order to produce is a kind of question -- so my own legal sense of fairness is not offended by placing it within 77(A) but if one prefers simply to make it prospective and a rule for the case, that is one alternative. The second alternative is to go to the Tribunal as a whole and craft a few rule. The principle is there. It is not a question of deviation from what has been the recognised authority of the Tribunal to compel the production of evidence, whether it is viva voce testimony or real evidence, the murder weapon, or documents that go to the heart of the defence charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Of course, we would also have to advise -- let me see if I can find 77 -- advise -- I was looking for the Rule that deals with advising the witness of his right not to incriminate himself. Let us see. Well, we will leave that aside. Anyway, according to your -- in your interpretation it would fit within 77(A)? One final question regarding national security claims. In your brief you take the position that a state may not make a blanket objection, that they can be required at least to provide the documents to the Trial Chamber for in camera review. You suggest advising procedures like the ones in -- is it CIPA?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: The Classified Information Procedures Act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Since you are an American lawyer, does Reynolds support that proposition that the Tribunal may compel the production of documents for review by the Chamber in camera even in the face of an objection on the basis of national security?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: The analogy to national law is not complete obviously, and there are unique problems internationally because ordinarily, as has been pointed out, it is the executive branch of the government that is making the weighing between the national security interests at stake and the interest in the enforcement of criminal law. Although in the US, in fact, from time to time with the special Prosecutor Act, when you have independent arms, independent prosecutors created who are separate from the defence branch of the government, you get something of the same kind of problem, but CIPA has been very useful in finding a middle ground and mitigating the conflict. Early in the 80s or late 70s there was a great problem in Washington about so-called greymail where certain cases seemed untryable because the idea of an uncontrolled trial procedure where something might just pop out and something crucial to national security might just be blurted out by a witness was unacceptable. Therefore the idea of having very graduated procedures where you had to give notice of your intention to use classified information, protective orders, closed hearings, secure custodians and secure respositories went a very long way to mitigating any real conflict. There might ultimately be a question of a crucial particle of information that was both probative and yet prejudicial to a country's future national security posture, and in that case I guess I would expect it might well never come up, because a reasonable prosecutor and a reasonable national representative should be able to find some way to compromise that with the generic substitution of information stipulations. If it did come up then it would be for the Tribunal to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, it may for the Prosecutor and we do have a rule that somewhat touches that. It is 66 something or other. It is the last paragraph in 66, C or D -- C, but that is when the Prosecutor has, I gather, obtained state secrets from a state and then the Prosecutor wants -- has to really give assurances to the state that it will not disclose those state secrets. What about the defence, though? When the defence is seeking documents that may be relevant to his position and necessary for his defence, he is in a different situation. You do not have a question of a reasonable prosecutor and a reasonable state. You have a question of a defence lawyer who will do whatever he has to do to represent his client.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: There have been reasonable defence counsel in the past and I am sure in the future and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am not suggesting they were not reasonable but I mean that they have different interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: Under CIPA it has been handled with solemn bare-teethed protective orders in closed hearings, a high standard of materiality and admissibility. You can't have any old piece of information. You have to show why it is necessary to your case. But the number of actual conflicts have been relatively small. Under the Totten case in the US -- I mean from time to time there are cases that become untryable. It is 1875. I will give your Honour the citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The year 1875. No wonder I have forgotten it. I have a long memory but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: The Totten doctrine came up more recently in the Home Port litigation before Judge Sifton where a question of environmental impact statements and whether the navy was nuclear or not if they adopted Staten Island. Occasionally there are cases that become untryable, because the information is that sensitive, but this is retrospective, number one. Number two, if you take the national security exception at any great breadth, the very nature of war crimes would become untryable. Again to prove command responsibility even by the defendants' lights, you have to show what went on in a military headquarters. So any kind of blunderbuss blanket automatic national security exception would gut and disembowel the very idea of command responsibility. So it requires a sensitive approach by the court which I simply thought CIPA might produce some analogies for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The national security claim would always act against the accused. The prosecution cannot get the evidence if it has no case, but it is the accused who is going to suffer, because there may be some documents which have a bearing on his defence. So in practice it is the accused who is going to suffer because it is a national security claim. In fact, you are leaving the fate of the accused not to the Tribunal but to the state which is claiming -- placing a claim for national security. It is the accused who will always suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: It may cut both ways, your Honour. If there was an order by an accused saying: "Please do not harm that villager"; it would clearly be exculpatory. if the records, however, showed he had failed to set up a decent reporting system for his men in the field, it would be inculpatory. It may cut both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So if it is for the prosecution to prove the case and the prosecution is unable to get that evidence, there is no case for the accused to answer, but the accused, if he has no access to exculpatory documents he suffers in his defence. So how can there be a proper trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: That is very fair, your Honour. I mean, I will sit down, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: In some instances we would have to dismiss the indictment if we found that the evidence -- Mr Hayman was dosing there but he heard that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I heard you perfectly clearly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You were not dosing; you were sitting back. If it is necessary, if he is unable, if it is critical to his defence, I guess there will have to be a determination.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: I do think some of the innovations of this Tribunal on an anonymous witnesses, even though it was controversial to the academic community, but still some of the sensitive procedures that this Tribunal has devised for treating the very personal interests and -- against the interests of justice that arise in these cases, the same acumen and surgical technique can be applied to this as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am glad you mentioned that, because just in terms of dealing with hearing witnesses, we have devised a number of very creative protective measures for both prosecution and defence, unknown in national systems, again cognisant of the particular situation that we have, so maybe we ought to use that same kind of creativity at this time. I had not thought about it. Thank you. Do you have anything else, Miss Wedgwood?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEDGWOOD
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Prosecution, do you have anything in rebuttal? JUSTICE ARBOUR: I do, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You may proceed. So much has been said. JUSTICE ARBOUR: I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Take your time. Rebuttal presentation by Justice Arbour JUSTICE ARBOUR: I merely have several rebuttal issues to raise particularly in respect of submissions that have been made by representatives of the Republic of Croatia. If I may, at the outset I would like to address the three broad submissions of law and policy that were put forward by Ambassador Simonovic this morning. The first point I would like to make is that the Security Council was very clear that it did not wish to create any new substantive humanitarian law. That was made very clear in the deliberations of the Security Council. In my submission, it was equally clear that it wished to create an effective international criminal court to which it would delegate all the powers to make its own rules of procedure and evidence. So, in my submission, the creation of new law was a matter of substantive law, not a matter of procedure and evidence. My second submission relates to the argument that was put forward in morning that the duty to cooperate on the part of states is sufficient for this Tribunal to operate effectively as a criminal court. To this I merely wish to point out that in reality most of the time this is accurate, that the obligation to cooperate on the part of states goes a long way to rendering this Tribunal perfectly sufficiently efficient in the discharge of its mandate. I wish to point out, however, that the duty that is imposed on states by the Security Council in creating the Tribunal is not merely the duty to cooperate. That is only Article 29, Subsection 1. Article 29, Subsection 2, which is the sole one that we are interested in these proceedings, is not the duty to cooperate; it is the duty to comply with orders. That duty was wisely imposed by the Security Council, realising that in law, if not merely in reality, the duty to cooperate is likely to be insufficient. This is rendered evident in this particular case that the duty to cooperate is not sufficient, and I will give two examples which illustrate the point. The question was raised this morning as to whether or not the Republic of Croatia had, in fact, appointed a person to assist in cooperation with the Tribunal, and I merely wish to point out that the person who has been appointed as the head of office for cooperation is Dr Jelanic, who is the signatory of the brief which contains the threat to cease future cooperation with the Tribunal, should the decision not be acceptable to Croatia, a statement that has not been withdrawn by the Republic of Croatia. Furthermore, this court has found in their Rule 61 decision in the Rijic case, and I will merely read the conclusion, the last conclusion reached by this Tribunal: "The Tribunal notes that the failure to affect personal service of the indictment can be ascribed to the refusal to cooperate with the International Tribunal by the Republic of Croatia and by the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and entrust the responsibility of so informing the Security Council to the President of the International Tribunal". There is thus a precedent which clearly demonstrates that the simple duty to cooperate was wisely determined by the Security Council to be an insufficient means of ensuring the effectiveness of this Tribunal. The last point that was raised by Mr Simonovic was whether or not to entrust this Tribunal with powers of compellability of evidence would threaten the growth in future of enforcement of international humanitarian law, the suggestion being that such powers would threaten the feasibility of contemplating that there would be one day a permanent international criminal court. In my submission, there is a greater threat to the growth of enforcement of international humanitarian law, and that would be a demonstration that this ad hoc Tribunal was not only impotent but was vulnerable in reaching accurate factual conclusions in the discharge of its mandate by being at the mercy of the capricious discharge by some states of their obligations to cooperate and to comply. So, therefore, in my submission, this is not a policy issue that should be given any serious consideration. I now wish to address briefly the question of the subpoena being a procedure solely borrowed from US law and misunderstood as that by the Prosecution. If I may refer the court to the Criminal Code of Canada, one that I am particularly familiar with, as we tend to turn to our own national system, if not to suggest they are determinative, but for some guidance, Section 699 of the Canadian Criminal Code provides: "Where a person is required to attend to give evidence before a Superior Court of Criminal Jurisdiction, a Court of Appeal, an Appeal Court or a Court of Criminal Jurisdiction ..." I will spare you a description of what these all are, but they are all criminal courts: "... a subpoena directed to that person shall be issued out of the court before which the attendance is required". Section 700 reads as follows: "A subpoena shall require the person to whom it is directed to attend at a time and place to be stated in the subpoena to give evidence and, if required, to bring with him anything that he has in his possession or under his control relating to the subject matter of the proceedings". I wish to point out that Canadian criminal law is not derivative of American law, but indeed is derivative, as are most criminal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is the other way round, you would suggest, is it not? JUSTICE ARBOUR: It is derivative, as we well know it, as is the criminal law of most former British colonies, of British common law and is in particular derived from Stephens' Draft Code, which was designed at the end of the 19th century, not adopted in England but adopted very broadly throughout the then British Empire, and therefore the correct reference to this proceeding is not to the law of the United States or any particular feature of that jurisdiction, but indeed is a very broadly used method of compelling attendance and production of evidence throughout countries that share a common law background. I will merely add that to the extent that it has some reference to the law of the United States, the retrenchment that has been referred to in the United States relates to the use of subpoena for discovery purposes. I do not want to repeat my earlier submissions that the subpoenas that are sought in this particular case relate to the production of evidence for trial purposes. This is not a discovery exercise, so I will distinguish it on that basis. Even though the subpoena is a uniquely common law-type mechanism of compellability of evidence, we have made references to various other countries that are not rooted in the common law, such as Spain and France, where analogous powers of compellability are always present. They are analogous merely in the sense that the court has at its disposal means to ensure that it will obtain the evidence. The mechanisms for so achieving are vastly different, but the intent, the spirit of what is achieved, is the same. We have several of these references. One has been made in the case of Germany, and I will merely correct any misconception that might have been reached by that reference in just pointing out, if I may -- that is right. The reference was made to an exception in German criminal procedure law respecting the filing in court of official state documents. That, in fact, is the provision that relates to any kind of national security exception. What we have submitted in our material is the broader scope under German criminal procedure law, which begins at Section 48, which contemplates that witnesses are to be summoned to give their evidence. It also contains what I have alluded to as probably a desirable practice of ensuring that the summons contains a reference to the legal consequence of failure to appear, but the German Procedural Code then carries on indeed to state that even the President of the Federal Republic is compellable to give evidence, although it provides for a different mechanism for his or her evidence to be taken. Then it provides for a consequence of failure to appear and so on, which contains penal consequences, as it tends to do in most legal systems. The form, in my submission, of the order that has been issued in this case is entirely provided for in the Rules, and the substance is entirely provided for by the Security Council in the Resolution creating this Tribunal. The Republic of Croatia through its counsel this morning conceded the Tribunal's power to compel the attendance of witnesses. Now, that being the case, and we have made submissions that there is an indistinguishable power to compel the evidence from the state based on the obligation of the state to comply with the Tribunal's order, and a Decision, of course, by the Tribunal that the order is indeed required for an expeditious and fair disposal of the case, now that being so, I submit that there is no basis upon which to distinguish and put so-called high state officials in any different category than all other natural persons. In my submission persons and states share the same obligation. The only issue is: who shares in the different penalty or enforcement mechanism? There is no reason to suggest that the state has any immunity from compliance to pass down to its officials. It is not immune from compliance. It may be immune under the current regime that we have from seeing itself the target of the imposition of a fine, for instance, because nothing in the rules so provides, but it is certainly not immune from compliance. Therefore, it has no such immunity to pass to its officials. Therefore, in my submission, all share in the same duty to comply, and all natural persons should be treated the same way when it comes to mechanisms of enforcement. I also wish to point out that neither, as far as I could tell, in international law nor in any other basis is there such a category as "high government officials." If there was to be a difference of treatment, it would have to be a difference of treatment that would fall upon government agents, all public servants. There is no legal distinction that would guarantee a difference in treatment in a government official holding a particular rank in the system, as far as I can ascertain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just one moment. Is it fair to an individual who happens to be the Director of Security -- I am just making up a title -- is it fair to him to be penalised, subject to potential imprisonment and a significant fine, when his state cannot be fined? Do you understand what I mean? You issue a subpoena to the state and they say: "We will not comply". You say: "Thank you. We will go to the Security Council and ask them to put that on the agenda". Then with the individual we find him in contempt, sentence him to six months and fine him $10,000 and he says: "Well, you know, I could not do anything. I am only the director of ..." -- whatever I said he was -- "I am the Director of Security". It seems a little unfair, does it not? JUSTICE ARBOUR: It seems so unfair I would not contemplate that this Tribunal would reach that conclusion. If a government official appeared before the court in response to a subpoena and made that statement, that is: "I did not bring the documents and I cannot give you any evidence, because my government will not allow me to do so", it may very well be that the Tribunal in fairness would say -- would refrain from exercising any more duress on that person, and then put the blame where it lies, on the government. That is one option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It would not be contumacious refusal. It is the contumacious refusal which is punishable. JUSTICE ARBOUR: That is right. It is the disrespect of the court and bringing the court into disrepute. It could be considered -- that is essentially the point -- as any other excuse. It may or may not in a given case have sufficient credibility and weight to excuse the person from the failure, but the failure, in my submission, would not be contumacious if the person was in an impossibility, either physical or in some sense moral. If the person, for instance, said: "You could either put me in jail here for six months, or I will go home and get the documents and serve six months there for violating domestic law ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You are assuming this is a world where people are allowed to move freely and impediments are not placed on their movements. I would imagine, if I were the Director of Security and a subpoena was addressed to the Deputy Director, that that Deputy Director would not come. He would not appear. So that Deputy Director would never have the opportunity to come to this Tribunal and explain: "I would have complied but my supervisor would not allow me". What we are doing then is in his absence holding him in contempt, fining him and putting potentially very significant restriction on his future liberty. He may want to take a trip to Switzerland and he might have difficulty doing that, simply because he is obeying his boss, but his boss is not only telling him: "Do not produce, but you do not leave this country", which does not seem too far-fetched to me. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Well, again I submitted yesterday that it certainly would not be wise practice, even assuming that that is what the rules contemplate, to proceed to a finding of contempt and the imposition of a penalty in the absence of the witness. In my submission the best practice is to then issue a second order compelling the state to produce the witness. That may be called issuing a warrant for arrest. It could be called issuing a request for the state to assist the Tribunal in bringing one of its citizens to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, and to leave it at that, thereby not having to face this kind of dilemma and visiting the responsibility then where it really lies, on the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Are we making then too much of this? What do you, since you are the party -- and the defence also asked for documents to be produced -- do you really expect to get anything from this as a practical matter in the face of a recalcitrant state, or are we just arguing very interesting intellectual points that have resulted in thirteen amici briefs and famous professors appearing? Are you really going to get anything if the state does not want to comply? You will say that we do not have the power to fine the state or hold them in contempt, but instead just report to the Security Council. You say if the Deputy Director of Security does not appear because, of course, the Director is not going to let him come, we would not hold him in contempt. Are we not just spinning our wheels in a sense? JUSTICE ARBOUR: At the end of the day I am not extremely optimistic we would get very much from states who consistently and defiantly refuse to cooperate with the Tribune, and I will have to concede that much, but that would not be a reason, in my submission, to shy away from an interpretation of the Statute that is entirely open to this Tribunal to find, and frankly there may be some considerable gains in addressing the subpoena to the custodians of the documents in question, some of which -- some of whom may be willing to come to the Tribunal, even at the risk of resigning their functions, or at some personal consequences in the same way -- maybe more dramatically so -- in the same way, I submit, that witnesses are called to come to give their evidence in a criminal forum, who, left to their own device and completely left alone, might very well choose not to do so. There are grave and sometimes adverse consequences felt by witnesses as a result of being compelled to give their testimony. People are compelled to testify against their family members. It can jeopardise personal relationships, professional relationships. It may be disadvantageous in many respects, and yet we certainly would not yield the compellability power because of these reasons. So, in my submission, the fact that there may be many circumstances in which a high government official or any other government official might be reluctant to defy the orders by his state to refuse to comply with an order would not be sufficient for this Tribunal to abdicate a power that it, in fact, should be asserting very vigorously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It might also enable the Tribunal, should it adopt such a procedure and should it be -- but I am very optimistic -- that states -- should it be that states again fail to comply, it may be a way to advise the Security Council with greater specificity just what is happening rather than a simple report of non-compliance of failure to execute an arrest warrant. Instead it would be a report to the Security Council, assuming this is part of the package, that: "We have attempted to discharge our judicial functions. We have had someone in custody for 12 months and here we are being pulled back and forth by a state, or two states, or three states because of their refusal to provide what both parties contend are documents that are essential to the trial". Meanwhile a person sits with his liberty curtailed, which is a very serious matter. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Indeed I think one could view that as an escalation of non-compliance from an official to an act of commission. It is one thing for a state merely to not comply with an order; it would be another matter altogether for the Tribunal to report to the Security Council that a state is not only not complying with orders issued to it but is actually taking active positive steps to prevent government employees from complying with the orders. So I think it would aggravate the illegality of the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have gone past our time normally for recess, because we were so involved in the discussion, and I have been rightfully advised it is time for us to recess for twenty minutes. We will recess until 4.30. (4.10pm) (Short break) (4.30pm) JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Madam Arbour, before going further I would like to ask you something. I have been listening about the difficulty that the Croatian Government has with the use of the world "subpoena" and even worse with the expression "subpoena duces tecum". I would like to ask you your opinion about this. As you know better than that, we have two working languages in this Tribunal, and the Article 54 in French has different words. It says "ordinances, citations a comparaitre, assignations". Do you not think that perhaps if you issue a text in French instead of English the problem could be solved? It is an idea. I am trying to be helpful. JUSTICE ARBOUR: Indeed it is extremely helpful to find the French version, particularly since the word "assignations" is also found in the French Code of Criminal Procedure dealing with not all methods of compelling attendance of witnesses but certainly dealing with -- "assignations a comparaitre" is an expression that is found in that legislative instrument. I should point out, however, I am somewhat puzzled at the suggestion that the expression "subpoena duces tecum" is English. It is Latin. One might have found exactly the same one in all languages. In any event, the position I take with that is that it is an expression that is found in the Rules, and it is an error to read into that word a whole legal content that may come from one or another particular national jurisdiction. The fact that in French it is called "assignation" I think shows it does not necessarily by its mere terminology contain the threat of the imposition of a penalty. However, my ultimate submission on that point is that there is, in fact, a penalty for non-compliance, one that is probably much more effective when applied against a state than a fine would be, even a substantial fine, and that is the public denunciation of the failure to comply. It is absolutely clear that before reporting to the Security Council, this Tribunal would make the finding of fact, and in my submission the finding of fact would be binding on the Security Council, that there is non-compliance with a validly issued order by this Tribunal. So there would not be any possible debate in the Security Council as to what occurred. There could be or could not be some debate as to what could be done about it. In my submission that is a penalty, if it is to be characterised as such, that is actually not inadequate concerning a state, but it certainly reinforces my submission that we cannot read anything into the usage of a particular expression. It has to be read in context. My final submission deals with the issue -- follows from my previous submissions dealing with the compellability of state officials, and I have to say that we have explored in these two days of arguments several possible scenarios. The one that I think would have never had a sufficient air of reality to be contemplated is the one we are actually facing today before this Tribunal, that is the case where a state asserts its intention to comply and concedes that it is bound by the orders issued by the Tribunal, and yet its Minister of Defence refuses, or so it appears, to obey by the order, a situation that I would have thought might have been difficult to contemplate, if we were not actually facing it. To the extent that there is any difference between a natural person and a natural person who has an official capacity, and I certainly do not concede that there is any such distinction, but if there was one, it would be, in my submission, entirely inapplicable to the Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, since his own state does not purport to confer upon him any possible immunity that it may have asserted it had -- quite the opposite: the state concedes that it is bound and presumably -- not presumably -- admittedly it concedes that its officials are also bound to comply with the orders of this Tribunal. So quite apart from the question of law, as a matter of fact in this case it is my submission that the Minister of Defence for the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, his submissions cannot prevail. My final submission, just in conclusion, is that issues of enforcement are not dispositive of issues of entitlement. That fact that there may be some perceived difficulties in fact or in law in having proper enforcement mechanisms should not drive the analysis of whether or not this court should have the power that all criminal courts must have to compel testimonial and documentary evidence. So to the extent that there may be any concern with enforcement powers, it should be analysed completely separately and certainly should not lead to a conclusion that the compellability powers should be somewhat diluted in that respect. Unless you have any questions, these are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have no questions. Thank you. Mr Rivkin? Rebuttal presentation by Mr Rivkin

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I would like to thank you, Madam Chairperson and all your Honours, for your extreme indulgence in structuring flexible procedures. We certainly appreciate that. I also wanted to mention -- and I will try to be brief -- however, given a couple of points raised by the Prosecutor, His Excellency, Professor Simonovic, wanted to make a couple of brief remarks. We were frankly rather puzzled by the Prosecutor's attempt, joined by some of her amici, to recharacterise the issue before the Tribunal. The Prosecutor asked the Tribunal to issue a subpoena duces tecum to Croatia, and she filed a brief, styled a Prosecutor's brief, in support of the subpoena duces tecum. Not being a French speaker, I cannot fully discuss how one can translate "assignation", but let us just say that that is not the language that was used in her document. Let me just briefly cite from her brief. In her brief the Prosecutor characterised the issues before this Honourable Tribunal based on its own March 7 Order as follows: "The power of a judge or Trial Chamber to make the request to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a sovereign state. 2. The power of a judge or Trial Chamber" -- excuse me. There is an obviously conflict between trying to be fast and the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I want you to take your time. We plan on adjourning at 5.30, but we can go until we finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. "To make a request to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a high government official or state". Let me also say that the words "high government official or state" was the words used by the Prosecutor. We will be happy to join in the discussion of what are the differences among state officials based on their rank. "3. The appropriate remedies to be taken if there is a non-compliance of a subpoena duces tecum by a judge at Trial Chamber". Prosecutor's brief, pages 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Actually, Mr Rivkin, I framed those issues and I framed them from the bench. Perhaps if I had had more time, I would have done it with greater clarity, although I am kind of satisfied with those issues. At least those were the issues that I was concerned with at the time. So I framed those issues and directed the parties to brief those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, your Honour. Indeed, these are issues we have been addressing ourselves. Nevertheless, at least my impression, with all due respect, having listened to two days of proceedings, is both the Prosecutor and a number of amici are perhaps concerned about the absence of a word "subpoena", and not just "subpoena" but "subpoena duces tecum" in the Tribunal's Statute and its Rule. We have heard a lot of discussion that what is really involved here is an order for production of evidence, which, as the Prosecutor assert, the Tribunal can clearly issue. Let me state clearly that Croatia's objection here is not merely to the use of the word "subpoena duces tecum" rather than the word "order". This is not merely a matter of form over substance, and I certainly do not want you to think that we just have inordinate attachment to archaic forms which in may ways went out of our legal system certainly by late 19th century. As we understand it, the Prosecutor claims and continues to claim that the Tribunal has the authority to issue a binding -- we do not have a problem with "binding" -- coercive order to Croatia requiring the production of certain documents in its possession, and that if Croatia fails to produce these materials, its officials may be sanctioned for fines or imprisonment. That, of course, is the proper definition of a subpoena duces tecum and that is the definition the Prosecutor herself has cited in her brief. In fact, at page 12 of her brief the Prosecutor defines a subpoena duces tecum as an order "... compelling production of certain specific documents and other items", referring to Black's Law Dictionary, which is the definition of a subpoena duces tecum. The question here is precisely whether the process in issue is coercive with respect to a sovereign state. Croatia's position is, and it is only our position, that it may not be. This is the form that the Prosecutor has chosen to adopt and we argue that form matters. This is a court of law, not a therapy session where one is encouraged to express oneself in any way that one finds desirable. In fact, I am puzzled that a number of people, including some amici, have argued as well as the Prosecutor that forms are not that important. I would argue on behalf of our profession that format is a great deal in law and in international law in particular, where protecting the dignity of equal and sovereign states is an important imperative of the first order that is conducive both to the development of international law and to international stability. The Prosecutor now accepts that the Tribunal cannot issue a compulsory order, ie an order backed by coercion as distinct from a legally binding order for production of documents, however it is styled, and it can only issue a request for assistance under Article 29 or even an order, but without compulsion involved and frankly we can all go home. We would move that you quash the subpoena, rule that the Tribunal cannot issue a subpoena duces tecum. If the Prosecutor or the Tribunal want to issue an order requiring Croatia to produce certain documents, or argues that Croatia has an obligation to comply with such an order, Croatia is willing to work with the Prosecutor in complying with such a request. It is not my intention here to delve into factual issues because, in fact, the way you styled, very properly, this argument, your Honour, it is an argument about matters of law and not fact, but I am compelled to point out nevertheless in light of numerous assertions that have been made that Croatia has already cooperated quite extensively with this Prosecutor and the Tribunal, probably more extensively in Croatia's view than any other state. However, it is our view that neither the Prosecutor nor the Tribunal may compel for the use of coercive process and the imposition of sanctions Croatia to produce the documents in its possession. Let me move on to the next issue. We are also amazed that the Prosecutor in her argument at least for a certain time seemed to confuse subpoena duces tecum and subpoena ad testificandum, and I apologise for my Latin if it is not quite correct. At least as we understand it, a subpoena ad testificandum is merely a subpoena to testify. It is a technical and descriptive term for an ordinary subpoena as opposed to the subpoena duces tecum, which commands the production of documents. Again I am citing Black's Law Dictionary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: One of the amici, I think, cited -- I do not know which one it was -- a reference to -- it was probably in Frowein's brief, where some court had interpreted the two terms and said that one was implicit in the other. I think it was the subpoena to testify -- being implicit in that is the subpoena to produce documents. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I do not recall who said it, but yes, I recall that statement. Your Honour, we think -- and we would be happy to brief this issue for you -- we think it is an important distinction. In fact, I would say both subpoena ad testificandum and subpoena duces tecum are two different species, and not to belabour American law, since we have told, quite correctly, that that is the only mother load of all wisdom, in American law there is, nevertheless, I would like to mention, an important difference between having a witness bring several specific documents in his or her possession, so that he or she can be impeached, their memory can be refreshed, versus having a broad in essence fishing expedition dragnet type subpoena, and I would argue that subpoena duces tecum emphatically is not the proper legal process for saying: "Please, Mr John and Mr Fred, come to the court room and bring the following tape or bring the following diary entry". That is not the case here. I will just elaborate on that very briefly, because I was just going to get into it. This is a distinction with a difference. As I mentioned, the subpoena ad testificandum is directed at an individual who has or is believed to have personal knowledge about the facts in issue. Croatia, of course, is not an individual and cannot be summoned to give evidence as a witness. The individuals who the Prosecutor seeks to sanction are also not sought as witnesses who may give evidence based upon their personal knowledge. Let me just perhaps in response, your Honour, to your point about blending the common and civil law system say that my only problem, with all due respect to that, is that blending implies that they are two different species of subpoenas and two different systems and they are sort of usage-wise invoked with roughly similar frequency and you are trying to blend them. I do not believe that anyone has argued there is that case at all. You have few jurisdictions that use subpoenas and most of them do not. So it is not a case of blending. To me, with all due respect, if the legal process in issue does not partake of the features of a subpoena duces tecum, we should not call it a subpoena duces tecum; otherwise we sort of have an Alice-in-Wonderland problem. If there is spare time, I would not give a citation from there, but I am sure you know what I am referring to. One final point here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think it was Mr Condorelli who said that basically this is a blending of criminal concepts and concepts under international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think that is what he said in his brief. So perhaps that is the blending. So what he was saying is that this concept of a subpoena duces tecum is something that is unknown in international law, but is something that is known in criminal law, and that perhaps the Statute being drafted with some time constraints perhaps combines both concepts, or maybe I am misreading what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: No, I agree with that statement, your Honour, but perhaps I should add at this point in time that again, mindful of a number of excellent questions you asked, asking -- if I may paraphrase, and correct me if I am wrong -- "What is so special about a subpoena duces tecum? If we are going to take the matter to the Security Council, if we styled it as an order, what is the difference?", I would argue again, the word being used in its ordinary, normal usage, there is a certain degree of odiousness, a certain degree of compulsion, a certain degree of coercion that attaches to this particular term, which would not attach to the term "order". In our judgement, using the process when one really means an order addressed to the sovereign state of Croatia is a little bit unfair, because in some ways, irrespective of what is done at the Security Council level -- we have no doubt that the Security Council would back this distinguished Tribunal -- it would be difficult to get rid of that odious implication. Let us say, for example, you chose not to take the matter up to the Security Council. Having used that term, again from my own perspective, it is certainly prejudicial in a court of public opinion. Again not to be too parochial here, but I would remind you of a number of statements made by people, like the case of Secretary Donovan in the Reagan administration, who, after being acquitted of all the charges by the independent council, said rather mournfully: "Where do I get my reputation back?" It is a situation where there is a degree of sanction, a degree of opprobrium here that the state of Croatia would never be able to fully eradicate, no matter what happens. That is indeed one manifestation of a problem of using this very specific term. If I may proceed, in our opinion the real reason, and not a very good reason, why the term subpoena duces tecum is used is because the Prosecutor understands very well that styling something as an order addressed to a sovereign state presents a real problem of imposition of individual liability on government officials, and I will be happy to address it in a second. However, in most jurisdictions that do use the word subpoena duces tecum, it is in general understood that when such a subpoena is directed at a corporate entity, individual liability may apply. In our view it is not just a matter of formulation. It is a choice designed precisely to get at a result and the appropriate result that in our view the Prosecutor seeks.
