Again, let me briefly address the question which has been discussed here rather extensively about official capacities and whether or not being a state official is a bar. It is not a bar in any sense either appearing as a witness or as an accused. What we are trying to say is all those duties relate to one's individual conduct. If one is acting in official capacity, we find it difficult to understand, and I think I may have mentioned this point earlier. How can you sanction somebody for a conduct that is perfectly legal and perfectly appropriate? In fact, we would argue that an individual's official conduct in some perhaps metaphysical sense is not really the conduct of an individual; it is the conduct of a state. So in the hypothetical which the Prosecutor and you discussed the situation where you have a government official being asked to appear as a government official, and the superior government official telling him not to appear and this individual being put on the horns of a dilemma to decide which way to proceed, is he going to value his personal career above his obligation, to me it is a misnomer. An individual may not appear in his official capacity if his sovereign tells him not to appear, because by virtue of appearing in his official capacity he or she is the sovereign. So if a sovereign tells him not to appear, there is no duty -- I mean, it is not even theoretically possible, but again I will be happy to discuss this point, if you wish. The only way you can have an individual appear is as an individual, because of acts he committed as an individual or knowledge he has as an individual, and in no other way. We have heard a lot of discussions today about obligations and the various provisions of the Tribunal's Statute, with Articles 15, 19, 20, 21 being implicated as well as various Rules of the Tribunal, particularly Rules 54 and 77. I would argue that even the most tortured reading of these provisions does not support the Prosecutor's original demand for the issuance of a compulsory process in the form of a subpoena duces tecum against the sovereign state. In any case, as I think we have tried to argue, these provisions, as well as the others that have been discussed, cannot be construed in isolation. With all due respect to the principle of effectiveness, I think the overarching principle of legal construction of any document has to be done in the context of an overall grant of authority to a Tribunal, which itself must be construed within the overall structure of the UN Charter, which in turn has to be construed within the body of existing international law. In that regard I would also remind you that even the United States' constitution, which we certainly take very seriously, is construed within the context of certain pre-existing legal authorities, the common law of England, etc, etc. In that regard we believe that the Prosecutor has made three separate but essentially unsupportable assertions. Firstly, the Prosecutor correctly pointed out that there are no specific proscriptions in the Tribunal's Statute that forbid the issue of a subpoena duces tecum. We agree. That is perfectly clear. The Statute itself does not mention that particular process. However, we do not believe that the Prosecutor can correctly imply from this that the Tribunal has the power to issue a subpoena duces tecum. This is not a correct inference. The Tribunal is not a prerogative court, like English courts of the Star Chamber or High Commission. Rather, it is a court of limited jurisdiction and power, established by the Security Council for a specific purpose and object. Under Article 1 of the Tribunal's statute its competence is limited to: "Power to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 in accordance with the provisions of the present statute". If the Statute does not confer particular power upon the Tribunal, then the presumption must be the Tribunal does not have such a power. I will be happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Rivkin, suppose it was a high governmental official, whatever that means -- but we have all been using the term, I suppose, with some mutual understanding -- interferes with or intimidates a witness. 77(C) allows for the Tribunal explicitly to hold that person in contempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour -- I do not want to interrupt you, of course -- absolutely, because the first point here would be that you have the power explicitly, but more importantly, and again perhaps it is a legal and philosophical matter, intimidation of witnesses cannot possibly be within the province of official duty of any official. It is like saying: what if you have a government official that commits burglary or rapes somebody? Obviously those actions can never be a part of the official conduct of any sovereign, so you have got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Well, our subject matter jurisdiction speaks to command responsibilities -- let us not argue that point, but let us suppose a high governmental official interferes with a witness, and he has a significant position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: With all due respect, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We can hold him in contempt, can we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Even if he is acting as an agent of the state, we can hold him in contempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would argue that anybody acting that way cannot act as an agent of a state because certain actions -- as a matter of fact, if you look at Hughes and Bellow and International Law, Warren, and various protocols that have been codified, acting in that way is not an official act. Therefore your official status is no bar to it. Common law crimes, which certainly include intimidation of witnesses, can never be a part of one's official duties. My answer to you is you are absolutely on solid grounds, your Honour, for two reasons. First of all, you have specific language to deal with it, but, more importantly, that is not an act of a sovereign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If, for example, a captain was carrying out a design of his state for the annexation of a portion of another state, he would not be carrying out the design of the sovereign?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I would argue that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And pursuant to that design, that plan, he intimidates or threatens a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: If I may, I would argue, your Honour, that it is pretty well-established that a conduct of that nature is unlawful under international law. Following orders or acting as an agent of your sovereign is no defence indeed. Again, perhaps, it is an epistemological problem, but I would argue that anybody acting in a way that is clearly understood to violate the law of nations is not acting in official capacity. What he has received is an illegal order. That is, I believe, the holding of the judges in Nuremberg. That is the view incorporated into German law, that basically if you receive an order from your superior, but it is an unlawful -- that asks you to violate the law of war, of which humanitarian international law is certainly a part, you have not received a valid order. It is ultra vires, just like having the Tribunal issue an invalid order is ultra vires. So we never really get into a problem in this area. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You may continue. You should visit us, I suppose, as we proceed with some of our trials and see how we fare, but you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the Prosecutor's reasoning -- I am just trying to connect to my last point. Because the Statute does not allow a Tribunal to involve the Security Council's power to use military force against the state, it must be assumed the Tribunal has such power. In fact, there are courts that do have a power. They have marshalls assigned to them. They have a power to compel production of witnesses. There are courts that do not care how witnesses or accused get there. Some courts do. Some courts would not allow somebody -- as I am sure you know, your Honour, there is a serious problem in some US courts where people, for example, from Mexico have been illegally seized and brought before them, and some courts have taken the view: "We do not care how people got here. As long as you are here, that is fine". Other courts have not. All I am trying to say is that the power to use some direct form of coercion is not unknown to some tribunals. Are we to infer that the Tribunal has this power because the Statute does not expressly bar it? Again, in my opinion, that stands reason on its head. In fact, in our judgement it is particularly important to reject the Prosecutor's assertions, because the power being claimed here is the power to coerce sovereign states here for legal process and sanctions, which is the most fundamental matter and the very highest of the Security Council's own prerogatives. It should not be touched lightly. To the extent that the Security Council -- and perhaps I am just sort of restating the same point -- wanted to give this power to the Tribunal, given the nature of this power, it surely would have stated so with a degree of explicitness that probably would have caused us all not to be here today. Second, the Prosecutor continues to assert that the Tribunal must have a power to issue a subpoena duces tecum, because without this power, it would not be effective, and the Security Council wanted the Tribunal to be effective. I would argue, however, and again I do not want to get too much into a factual discussion, that the Prosecutor has failed to show why the Tribunal would be ineffective if it did not have this power. Listening to some of the questions asked by your Honours, my only answer is it surprises me why we have to look at things in very binary black and white terms. It is as if a Tribunal is either perfectly ineffectual, completely unable to proceed, or completely effectual. In fact, there are a lot of gradations in between. I would argue that your own record today demonstrates that you have been effectual, having indicted a number of people, having conducted a number of trials. I understand, and I do not want to be presumptuous to argue that things are proceeding as you would have liked, but there is certainly no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am not even going to respond to that. I could not begin to tell you my feelings about that, but what I wanted to comment on -- I was trying not to interrupt you -- Rule 54 was amended on January 30th, 1995, and we have many people who watch the Tribunal and write Articles. Professors write articles about what we do. The persons in the Legal Office of the United Nations write articles about what we do and the Rules that we draft. I have not seen any articles that have addressed this subpoena -- the adoption of the amendment in January of 1995. Have you? I would think, assuming that people are interested in what we are doing, and there are some people, that if it was so outrageous that some academicians and perhaps even some people in the Legal Office in the UN would have said: "Now, wait a minute! Where did you get that power?" Really I have no idea whether things have been written about it. Do you know? Not that it makes a difference, because, you know, we read our press with the same, I suppose, degree that anyone in the public reads the press. Have you seen anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I have not, your Honour, and while I would not presume to tell you a great deal how to construe your own Rules, it seems to me again, coming from an American tradition, reading the Rules, that the word "subpoenas" and "summonses" and "orders" clearly applies -- or at least is not flagged as to apply to the states. That is the only problem that perhaps somewhat pedantically we keep coming back to. I would argue that if you promulgated a Rule, with all due respect to your Honour, that specifically stated that subpoena duces tecum would lie against the state, you would see a great deal of commentary on this issue. So perhaps people have not fully appreciated how the word "subpoena" in Rule 54 could be constrained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Again perhaps I am being unfair in re-characterising what the Prosecutor is trying to say, but again I do not fully appreciate the black and white zero sum game nature of the situation. I think what the Prosecutor is really saying, and actually factually I agree with her, that if the Tribunal had the power to issue a subpoena duces tecum, it would be more effective. This may or may not be true; it probably is true, but this is not a legal argument. Indeed, I think that this is not even an argument of necessity. It is an argument of expediency. With all due respect to the Prosecutor, I would not rank this argument as one that should find much hospitality in most courts of law. Clearly the Tribunal could be much more effective if it assumed any number of new corrosive powers not specifically granted to it by the Security Council. I am very mindful of all the things about how busy the Security Council is, as described by various amici. For example, the Tribunal's work would be much easier and more effective therefore to issue binding orders to states, and I do not mean state -- orders to produce documents, but if you issued orders to states that are members of SFOR, with troops now in Bosnia-Herzegovina, requiring them to apprehend and transport to The Hague certain major indicted war criminals who have been thumbing their nose at the international community, such people as Karadzic and Ladic, under the Prosecutor's logic the Tribunal clearly would have such a power, since the Security Council did not deny this power in the Statute. Maybe it is worth considering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We do have binding authority. I thought we had that binding authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Legally coercive orders to those troops. Probably again if one is to read the papers and believe what is there, there have been a number of encounters between the troops of various SFOR members in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where people who are clearly on the list drive past checkpoints and no efforts have been made to apprehend them. Maybe you should command that they be seized and issue the order to those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have issued arrest warrants and we asked for states to execute those. In some instances when states have failed to do that, we have then reported their failure of cooperation to the Security Council, and that has been the penalty that we imposed. We did not go out and seize them ourselves, if that is, I think, what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Right. Right. Moreover, despite the Prosecutor's claims that the Security Council has delegated the full plenitude of its powers to the Tribunal so that it may be effective, I would argue that there is no evidence either in the language of the Tribunal's Statute or in the Resolutions or other discussions surrounding the Tribunal's creation that the Security Council purported to vest this Tribunal of all the Chapter 7 powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do not think the Prosecutor takes that position. We will hear from the Prosecutor. That was a question that I asked to several people. I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: In that case I stand corrected, but let me just say then that there is no support for the proposition that the Security Council intended to vest the Tribunal of the most awesome of its powers, which is the taking of coercive action against the sovereign state. Indeed, it is far from clear to us, and I promise we will not get into a long discussion of how Chapter 7 works, but let me at least say that it is far from clear that the Security Council could have made such a delegation, since Chapter 7 of the UN Charter provides that it is the Security Council that may decide upon the measures necessary to address a threat to peace. I also note, and again if I mischaracterise what the Prosecutor said, please correct me, but I believe the Prosecutor actually suggests that not only has the Security Council vested the Tribunal with several of its awesome powers, but the Tribunal is also not subject to authority or control of the Security Council with regard to the performance of its judicial functions. I have no problem as long as those functions are judicial. To me and many other experts in international law exerting coercion against sovereign states is essentially not a judicial action. It is, of course, a legal action in so far as it is undertaken in conformity with Chapter 7 of the UN Charter, to which all UN members have subscribed, surrendered the portion of their sovereignty. None of us has any problem with that proposition, but I would not argue it is a judicial power. It is not a judicial power in the sense that there is no recourse --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down a bit? JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You must slow down. I am listening to you so much I apologise for not noticing the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I apologise. I get carried away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you are not in the middle of a sentence, let me ask you a question. When the Security Council dispenses UNPROFOR, that is an enforcement measure; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They despatch them, send them somewhere and tell them: "You are the enforcement measure. Help to bring about peace". Do they supervise their activities and make any check on them to see whether they should take a left turn, a right turn, whether they truly should go into a particular community, that kind of action, or do they tell them: "You get the job done"?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they certainly do get the job done. In other circumstances I might be very tempted to discuss the delegation doctrine, certainly as it arose in American courts, but I would argue that there is a fundamental difference between delegating certainly a coercive/executive power to somebody else's troops, troops of a sovereign state that are serving under a UN flag, and telling them to do whatever is necessary -- in your hypothetical, which village to go to -- and endowing the Tribunal, which is a judicial body, a very powerful judicial body, but with all due respect a judicial body, with non-judicial powers, because to me -- and we will be happy to brief it in greater detail -- most international law scholars would believe it an agreeable proposition that taking coercive action against the sovereign state is a political, military exercise, not a judicial exercise. Making a state subject to legal duty is, of course, a judicial exercise. The coercive element is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Again reporting to the Security Council is a penalty of sorts. We have many citations in the briefs from the amici that even the pronouncement of non-cooperation is in itself a penalty. That is the power that we have taken upon ourselves and I do not think you challenged that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, with all due respect, of course we did not challenge your power to report people to the Security Council, but let me emphasise again that the circumstances and the form of that report is quite important. We feel, of course, there is a considerable amount of let me just say penalty that would go at least in the court of public opinion with you referring any state for non-complying behaviour to the Security Council. We do feel that styling the circumstances or characterising the circumstances that give rise to that referral as a failure to respond to subpoena duces tecum, which is understood at least in the English-speaking world to be a very specific, very coercive form of process, creates an undue hardship that the Security Council did not contemplate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: All of this sounds to me like a political argument. It sounds to me, although I have not observed the Security Council, I suppose, with the regularity that Miss Wedgwood has --

utterances.speaker: MR. RIFKIN
utterances.text: Which I do not claim, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: There is much discussion about, you know, what you call someone, how you end a letter, even, how you begin the letter, and again I was looking -- I thought I said it was paragraph 28 of the Secretary General's report, where he says -- and I heard what Mr Malanczuk said about the status of the report -- but he says that: "The Security Council is establishing an enforcement measure under Chapter 7, a subsidiary order within the terms of Article 29 of the Chapter but a judicial one. This organ would, of course, have to perform its functions independently of political considerations". That is why, for example, in the many hearings that we have had on the subpoena with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina, when I hear counsel tell me: "If you write him a letter, he will come", well, that is not something that courts engage in. That is something that is left for the political arena. We issue orders and we issue orders that have to be complied with. Now we may not have the power to penalise a state, but if we have the power to report non-compliance with a state, it seems to me it is appropriate for us to do that. We may be obligated, if we were in the political arena, to begin our letters with: "His or Her Excellency" and end it: "You have my best ...", however the letters are ended, but that is not the way we operate. I do not think that I should be called upon to write a letter to Mr Jelanic, to put it very straightforward, because we are a judicial institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I find absolutely -- I cannot in any way disagree with the very cogent words you just used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What I say is if we were to issue a subpoena, it is not that we mean any disrespect in the political sense. It is just that what we mean is that it is subject to a penalty, which may be reporting to the Security Council, and if that is not appreciated by people in the political world, that may be unfortunate. Maybe there needs to be an education process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, again with all due respect, what you have just said reminds me of your question to one of the amici, if I am not mistaken, about why not strip the word "subpoena duces tecum" of this unfortunate connotation that it is inherently -- well, that it has coercive character vis-à-vis its recipient, and again we are only talking about states. Why not tell people that this is really nothing more than just a form of order? I guess I would appeal to a very common sense argument. Why use a term of art that has acquired certain connotations for centuries of usage if you are not using it the way the term of art is used? Why not use the word "order"? Again, aside from the issue of liability of individual state officials of whatever rank, and I will deal with it shortly, we would not be here, your Honour, if what was in issue was an order issued to the sovereign state of Croatia. Again, I will certainly leave it to your discretion if you want to call it request for assistance or an order. How politely it is phrased, those are not legal issues; they are prudential issues. Of course, you are seized as a Tribunal of a power to issue an order and not say: "Please come here and talk to us". We would not go very far and I certainly do not put myself in the same category as one of the counsel for the defence you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think you say that the Prosecutor has not a sinister but a real motive for using the word "subpoena". Would you repeat that again? I guess it is to go to the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: In my judgement, again given the way the term "subpoena duces tecum" has been used and has operated in those jurisdictions that have invoked it, using it gives you the unique benefit that at least it does not seem illogical to suggest individual responsibility. If you style something, your Honour, as an order to the sovereign state of Croatia at least at the rhetorical, perceptual, declaratory level, whatever you want to call it, the leap of faith that one needs to buy into to get to a liability of state officials qua officials is quite a bit higher. I certainly do not want to impugn the Prosecutor's motives but it is a logical inference that the choice of the process here was not accidental. It was meant precisely to make it easier to hold state officials personally liable in their official capacity. That is my only point. I would actually disperse with some of our remarks, because you already elicited some of the information out of me through your very probing questions. Our only point is that again if a state, any state, fails to comply with your order, which that state and all states have a legal duty to, your recourse, discretionary judgement on your part, because I believe you do not, as we all agree -- it is not that you have a duty to report it to the Security Council, but you certainly have a power to report it to the Security Council; indeed it is the only recourse. Let me just say that perhaps, again in response to a parade of horribles that was mentioned by one of the amici as to you having to pop in and out of various proceedings to deal with this or that specific subpoena, that would not be the natural course of conduct for any trial court. You can do an interlocutory appeal type step. You can go to the Security Council and ask them to clarify/vest you with the power to issue subpoenas. If the Security Council does it in its wisdom, then there will be no reason to quibble about it in the course of individual trials. I do not think that it is very a realistic action to postulate, your Honour, that the only alternative is to have this matter come repeatedly to a very busy Security Council. We move briefly to the third point. In our judgement the Prosecutor has also argued, incorrectly, that the power to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a state can be predicated upon the right to a fair trial founded upon the Tribunal Statute. Again we feel that the Tribunal Statute must be read in full and in context. If you do not have a power under the Statute to issue subpoenas duces tecum, you do not have that power under all of the provisions of that Statute. It certainly would be anomalous to say the Tribunal did not vest you with that power generically, but you somehow can infer it from people's right to have a fair trial, and again if I can fall for just a second on American experiences, you know from your own experience, your Honour, the United States places enormous --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: -- stock on the opportunity of the accused to get a fair trial. I mean, most criminal lawyers would tell you, and you know it very well, that we would rather have a situation where 100 guilty parties go free than one innocent person gets accused. However, the right to receive a fair trial is an important imperative and the one you ultimately satisfy. In my judgement, if I may just -- you have not asked me that question specifically, but I heard you ask it to several amici -- if you are presented with a situation where you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You were going too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Forgive me. I will try to slow myself down. If you have a plethora of evidence against the given accused, and you are satisfied as triers of fact that that evidence is sufficient, and the accused comes in and says: "There is some exculpatory document somewhere out in the universe. Please get it for me", I would not be surprised if you would proceed forthwith and convict such an individual. On the other hand, if it is your view that the Prosecutor's case is sketchy, fragmentary and key pieces of evidence are lacking, then in the exercise of your judicial discretion you may decide to proceed otherwise. I guess my point is that you never have under any circumstances, even in domestic courts, a perfect access to all the evidence. That is no inherent bar to the ability to receive a fair trial, because I have infinite faith in your wisdom, sitting as a trial court, to look at the evidence and decide what is the fair way to proceed. So again I do not see how getting 100 per cent of all the evidence available out there in the universe is an indispensable indicia of getting a fair trial. Several other matters very briefly. Again people have backed off a little bit from the use of the word "culprit state", but I try not to get hung up on that. Nevertheless I believe that from the prospective of Croatia or any sovereign state it is very disturbing to see efforts to create an artificial distinction between Croatia's obligation to cooperate with the Tribunal and obligations of all other states. Again since the Prosecutor -- correct me if I am wrong -- does not seem to claim any more that Croatia is a culprit state, and we have not heard much about the distinction between coercive and mandatory powers, I will not dwell on it, except to say that the Security Council has not determined that Croatia poses a threat to peace. In none of the Security Council Resolutions leading to the establishment of the Tribunal is Croatia identified either as an aggressor state or a threat to peace. I do not believe it could have been so identified given the facts involved, etc, etc. In fact, again just a brief reminder that the Resolution 827 that established the Tribunal stated in the plainest possible language that all states should cooperate equally with the Tribunal. It did not single out any state or group of states for specific treatment. I will spare reading this provision, since I am sure everybody knows this by heart, but our view is, and we would very much like to get this point clarified, that under the founding documents of the Tribunal Croatia has exactly the same rights and responsibilities as each member state of the United Nations to cooperate, comply, respond, assist, whatever words your Honours would like to use. Consequently, if the Tribunal can require Croatia to comply with a subpoena duces tecum, it can require each and every other state to comply with such form of process, again whether it is at the request of a Prosecution or of a Defence, or even sua sponte, as you see fit to discharge your very wise rule regarding the right to fair trial. We see no particular differences among any of those subpoenas. If one fails, all should fail; if one stands, all should stand. Let me again respond perhaps in somewhat of a flip side of this argument, that suggestions by the Prosecutor and several of the amici that Croatia's nation security considerations and imperatives may be assessed and balanced by the Tribunal, we do not believe those considerations are founded. In fact, we see it as somewhat of a specific manifestation of a more general troubling assertion that the duties involved, although it is sufficiently distinct, are different here. Well, in general, since we believe the Tribunal lacks the power to issue a subpoena duces tecum, while the discussions about national security exceptions are quite serious, I am sure your Honour would agree with me that if the issue of a first order is answered in the negative, you do not even need to get to an exception, because for an exception to apply, you have to find that this form of process against the sovereign state is appropriate. Second, a number of people have mentioned the balancing performed by national courts and national security claims. We have read with interest discussions about CIPA and the way to balance national security considerations and criminal trials. We feel they are entirely inappropriate here, and perhaps I am not just reiterating the point that I actually heard you elicit in one of the questions. The situations are completely different, because in all of the national court cases the only proper issue is who makes the binding decision for the sovereign as to which way things ought to be balanced? In some state systems it can be the court. In another it can be the Parliament. In a third one it can be the President. They are all really different manifestations, different components of a same sovereign, so you never have a problem. The sovereign makes the decision. The sovereign does not coerce himself, although I gladly acknowledge the somewhat special problem posed in the American system by independent counsel. This is manifestly not the case here. In fact, if I remember correctly, your Honour, you at least asked one of the amici the question: "Is it true that a Tribunal, an International Tribunal, for that reason has inherently less of an ability to balance those considerations than a domestic court?" My answer is unequivocally "yes". My next point is that Croatia quite seriously resents the implication that it cannot properly balance its own national security needs with the imperatives of bringing to justice those who have perpetrated crimes against international norms in the former Yugoslavia. We think it is exactly the reverse. In fact, Croatia has far more interest than most states in seeing that all the individuals guilty of such crimes are brought to justice. Unlike the United States, Britain, France, Russia or most member states of the international community, Croatia and her citizens were victims of an aggression and war crimes that are the subject of this Tribunal's jurisdiction. Moreover, I would hazard a guess that, as a young state, Croatia is particularly desirous of demonstrating how seriously it takes its obligations to cooperate in international fora, provided appropriate forms and norms of international law are observed. So to the extent that Croatia ever invokes its national security considerations in responding to a legitimate request or properly styled order, it would do so for the most compelling reasons. It certainly would not do any less than any other sovereign state. Let me briefly conclude by making just a couple of points. Again perhaps I am reiterating what other amici and counsel have said. We urge you to consider carefully the serious nature of the issues before you now, and we certainly commend you both for proceeding in a very deliberative and cautious and judicial manner, for having this hearing for a quite protracted time, inviting a number of distinguished amici. At stake here is not merely the progress of this prosecution -- it is important, of course, but it is only one imperative -- nor even the success of this Tribunal, which is enormously important but is not the only imperative in this world. I wanted to clarify because the Prosecutor took some umbrage at that. Why is it our position that allowing -- the Tribunal judging itself as being seized of this power that is not expressly vested in it by the Security Council, why is it bad for the future of international law, and this is a pragmatic argument, your Honour, but if you may indulge me, I would hazard a guess that no state, large or small, presented with a situation in the future would agree, however they described their reasons for it, to the establishment of a Tribunal that may so exceed the explicit textural parameters of its grant, and in my judgement, since the work of this Tribunal and other similar Tribunals is enormously important to the future of international law, the fact that the states would be very reluctant to resort to this instrument is going to make things considerably worse. By the same token, to the extent that Tribunals like yours play a very important role in promoting international stability as the instruments of a reconciliation, I think we are talking about enormously serious adverse consequences. I really do not see this as a conflict between a dedicated internationalist, who wants to enlarge international laws domain, and some sticklers to archaic processes and forms, who are standing in the way. I see this debate, if it is resolved in the proper way, as something that most people who feel seriously about international law ought to support. I just wanted, before I turn it over to His Excellency Mr Simonovic, to just very briefly mention at least, because again I think you raised it several times, your Honour, that as far as the Dayton Agreement is concerned, our view is very simple. Article 9 of the Dayton Accord did not enlarge the caveat, qualify or alter the duties established by the Security Council under Resolution 827. I would believe that it is quite common in international practice to repeat the same obligation. In fact, the Security Council itself does it with considerable regularity. We believe that to argue otherwise amounts to an argument that Croatia or other members -- other signatories to Dayton have somehow surrendered their sovereignty or limited their sovereignty. One final point, if I may be allowed to. I just wanted to make a very quick response to a point by one of the distinguished amici regarding the argument that, since Herceg-Bosna was not a state, how can a state claim that the documents that perhaps originated in that state are properly its documents? I think your Honour knows very well from your experience as an American judge that what controls here is the substance of the documents. In fact, in the American system, and I believe other systems, you have documents generated by government consultants, contractors, even private parties, that a government can properly classify and regard as state interest. There is a famous case where somebody on his own came up with a design for an atomic weapon. That information was suppressed and classified and treated as information produced by somebody in the Defence Ministry. So it is the substance that controls here. I do not view the status of Herceg-Bosna or any issue here as of any consequence. Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ambassador Simonovic? Rebuttal Presentation by Mr Simonovic

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First I would refer to the Dayton Agreement. I am especially related to Dayton, because I assisted in its delivery at Dayton. Some things that have been said concerning Dayton worry me, because they are contrary both to the letter and to the spirit of the Dayton Agreement. First, let us resort to the letter of the Dayton Agreement. What I intend to do is to read literally all related to International Criminal Court -- to the Tribunal related in the text of the Dayton Agreement: "The parties shall cooperate fully with all entries involved in the implementation of this peace settlement as described in the annexes to this agreement, or which are otherwise authorised by the United Nations Security Council, pursuant to the obligation of all parties to cooperate in this investigation and prosecution of war crimes and other violations of international humanitarian law". That is it. There is not a single letter about the Tribunal in the framework agreement nor in any of the annexes. That is it. There is not a word "special obligation of the parties". There is no "unconditional cooperation", nothing. It just says: " ... pursuant to the obligation of all parties". So just referring to the already existing obligation of parties, not creating any new obligation. That might not worry me that much as that the idea of limiting the sovereignty is totally contrary to anything we were doing in Dayton. Dayton should be blamed for many things, but not for that. The whole idea of Dayton was to resurrect a state, to enable it to function with the help of the international community, to help Bosnia to regain its sovereignty, and not to limit sovereignty of the states that were present in Dayton. In fact, there has been a notion that there were some military arrangements that were reducing sovereignty in Dayton, and the only arrangement that existed was Annex 1B of the Dayton framework agreement, and I represented Croatia as the head of the delegation on negotiation on that particular annex, so I am rather familiar with it. The content of Annex 1B is just to make a balance between forces in the territory of the states participating in the Dayton Agreement, but not because of limiting of their sovereign rights, but because it has been done in whole Europe after the end of the Cold War and has not been done in Yugoslavia, because it was neither east nor west; so just participating in something that has already been achieved in Europe. So either it is a limitation of sovereignty of all European states, or it is not a limitation of sovereignty of Croatia and other states as well. Now, your Excellency, let me conclude by reiterating how much the Government of Croatia appreciates your decision to organise this hearing and to invite very respectable amici curiae to participate. It is a clear proof of openness of the court to reconsider even its own decisions. This hearing has proved not only that this court has many friends, many distinguished amici curiae, but also that those friends, at least most of them, are real friends of the court, friends who are willing to say also from time to time something that might be unpleasant, including to give a warning to the court of limitation of its powers. There has been an issue raised concerning duty of Croatia not only to cooperate but also to comply. It is out of question. Croatia has both a duty to cooperate and to comply, although it is much more pleasant to hear about cooperation than the need to comply, and I would like to emphasise that the work of Tribunal is, whatever we say, to quite an extent related to the successfulness of cooperation, which I believe shall improve and become even better. Just as an illustration, after subpoena that has been issued against the Government of Croatia has been transformed into request or order, Croatian started to fulfil its obligations, its duty contained -- it started to deliver the documents that were asked for and shall continue to do so. On the issue that has also been raised concerning all powers needed for the court to be efficient, we have said a lot, but I will just reduce myself to the very principle of the rule of law, which exactly means power, but power within the limitation of the law. Finally, I would like to condense the position of Croatia concerning the issue of subpoena. Our position is that the Tribunal should reject the subpoena and the use of subpoenas, because they are legally unfounded neither in Statute nor on the international law, and, secondly, if the Tribunal finds that it cannot be efficient without subpoena, it should turn to the Security Council not necessarily, since we heard it is a busy place and it really is, every time and each time, but ask for the amendment of the Statute. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If the Statute were amended and the word "subpoena" was put in there by the Security Council -- the Secretary-General and adopted by the Security Council, would that be a problem under international law, as you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMONOVIC
utterances.text: I am not authorised for such a speculation, but if Security Council would deliberate in this manner, I do not think that it would, but take it conditionally and just as an academic statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What do you think, Mr Rivkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I would say that it would -- I hate to speculate, but, on the other hand, my personal opinion would be that it would not be a violation of international law, because by definition the Security Council's powers acting as constitutor are almost unlimited, but I would argue, though, that it would not necessarily be a judicial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Judicial issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: It would not necessarily alter international law, because again it is almost extra legal in nature, in a sense of a sudden jolt, if you will, to the body of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The reason I ask you is not to ask you to speculate. It is just to determine what is the real source of your objection. The source is that it is not contained in the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Indeed, and as a number of individuals have pointed out to your Honour, by virtue of the UN Charter to which every member has subscribed, the Security Council is vested with this enormous power to do almost anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Prosecutor? JUSTICE ARBOUR: I have nothing to say in reply, your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Crawford? PROFESSOR CRAWFORD: If the Prosecutor has nothing to say, your Honour, I have nothing either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am sorry. Mr Crawford? The Prosecutor has nothing to add. Mr Crawford? Mr Hayman, I still do not know exactly where you fit into this scheme, but you are sitting on this side, you or Mr Nobilo, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I apologise. Miss Vidovic, do you have anything to add? MME VIDOVIC: No, your Honour, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Miss Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Rivkin, from listening to the presentation and reading the brief, it appears that Professor -- I do not know who wrote the brief -- Josipovic probably authored the brief, listening to his preparation, and in the letter that was written by Mr Jelanic, whom I have never met -- he is the gentleman who has been given the responsibility for cooperating with the Tribunal. I never met him, but in any case he has written me several letters, and in the letter he wrote he reserved the opportunity to make additional written submissions. Do you wish to make an addition written submission, Mr Rivkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, subject to such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How long do you need -- subject to what? I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I was just going to say subject to your inherent power with which we do not quibble to prescribe the size, style and the number of days to prepare it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How long do you think you would need? How does ten days sound? Fifteen days? Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Washington DC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So you have to go back to Washington. How much time do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: A month would be ideal, your Honour, but we are happy to settle for whatever you can grant us. Maybe something between two weeks and a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you made a submission, I imagine I would have to give the prosecution an opportunity to reply to that. I do not know how much time they would need. They would need to see your submission. I do want to hear from you on this point, Mr Hayman. I do not know exactly how to fashion it. When I entered my order the first time, I directed both parties to file their briefs by April 1st and the replies by the 11th, as I recall. The Prosecution has reminded me that Croatia is the moving party, and actually I incorrectly began with the Prosecutor; I should have began with Croatia. What do you suggest, Mr Rivkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we will be quite pleased if we could receive three weeks, say 100 page limitation, and I would even undertake, since you mentioned this Tribunal being quite flexible, I would even undertake to provide an early draft to the Prosecution at an earlier time, so the final polishing stage need not prevent them from proceeding with their response. We take the documents we file seriously. There is some time involved in checking citations and making sure everything looks ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I would say that we can provide -- while it is an unusual procedure, if both sides agree, we can provide a brief to the Prosecution within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr Rivkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I was just saying while it is an unusual procedure, I do not see a problem if both sides agree. We can only certainly provide the gist of our brief to the Prosecution within two weeks, with a final brief due in three weeks, say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How much time would you need to submit a reply, assuming you received it in two weeks? JUSTICE ARBOUR: Your Honour, we are in the midst of litigation. There will be a status conference in this matter tomorrow, I believe. It will be my submission after two days of hearing and very extensive submissions by a lot of amici in lots of amici briefs that the period of time that is requested is unreasonable in light of the on-going prosecution. I have no particular to any particular land or format but I must record my objection to that period of time. We, of course, have no idea what to anticipate, but we would undertake to respond to any new submissions within a week, and I would urge that no more than ten days be allocated to the new submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Mr Hayman, you have submitted a subpoena now that we have. This Chamber has it. As I indicated, I reviewed some time ago the subpoena and the motion that you filed with Judge Jorda and then compared the subpoena that you have now submitted. There are some differences, but we have not signed it, nor have we discussed it with you, because of the challenge that has been made by Croatia, and as well -- when I suspended the subpoena to Croatia, the Prosecution has asked that it be reinstated, and I deferred ruling on that until we rule on this issue. I am thinking, and I often think out loud and sometimes I am sorry about it, I wonder perhaps if we could go ahead with the subpoena that you have submitted, at least get it in the works.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have two concerns, your Honour. One is that my subpoena request not be held hostage by Mr Rivkin's request or by any other further briefing that may occur in this matter. I concur with the words of the Prosecutor that after two days of hearing -- certainly General Blaskic has been very patient and defence counsel has been very patient. This is his case. He filed a request for a subpoena in February of this year, and it has awaited these scholarly proceedings, which we are not saying were unnecessary, but his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No, it has not, Mr Hayman. He filed it. It was then submitted to Judge Jorda. You had a status conference on it and then, as I have said, you have submitted a new subpoena. The subpoena we have is not the one that you submitted to Judge Jorda, and we need to spend some time with you, or Judge Jan needs to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we submitted a supplement. I would not characterise it as a new subpoena. It is new material to be supplemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Rather than using such potential inflammatory terms, let us see if we can solve the problem. This is what I am thinking. I am thinking that if we could get your subpoena going, so to speak -- I am just thinking out loud -- if you can meet with Judge Jan, perhaps he can sign the subpoena, but he still has to resolve the same kind of matters that I may have to resolve if I sign a subpoena, at least get it in the works -- that is what is important to you. He is ready to meet with you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is very important. My first concern is that our request not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Held hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- delayed or held hostage to further briefing, etc, and it seems to me there is no reason because of the position taken by the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just wondering. The objection today is mainly to the use of the word "subpoena", but probably it is being said orders can be issued. Instead of "subpoena" we put "order" is issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina does not have an objection. I do not see why we cannot get yours going.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no particular affection for any particular term. So we are not bound to any term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Any form of process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any objection -- then, of course, the Prosecution has filed a motion to reinstate the subpoena addressed to Croatia, and I have no idea where you are in terms of the exchange of documents. What you said was that you have needed the subpoena in force in order to get the documents. JUSTICE ARBOUR: That is our position, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I imagine -- I was a judge before and this was the most distasteful task of everything that I ever had to do and that was to resolve discovery -- we will call them discovery -- I know you do not call it discovery dispute, but in essence there is a request and then there is a response, and then you go back and forth, but maybe I can sit down with the two of you, that is the Prosecution and Croatia, whomever the lawyer would be, and see where you are on this. Perhaps I can help to get you together. Mr Hayman, you can sit down. I think we can resolve yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I had two concerns. I can sit down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Go ahead. Give us your second concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The second concern, your Honour, is we have a trial setting conference tomorrow morning, and I do not think it would be appropriate for the Prosecutor to seek any delay in the trial date for General Blaskic based on the pendency of this matter. I cannot see after a year how they could claim this subpoena is material. If they would, I think it is very important for this Trial Chamber to at least bear that possibility in mind, or perhaps wait until tomorrow's hearing to set a time limitation or other schedule for further consideration of this matter, because I would very much regret if the trial date in General Blaskic's case is delayed because of a further briefing schedule in connection with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You, though, want action on your subpoena. You began your presentation this morning, I think it was, or was it yesterday -- I think it was this morning -- yes, it was this morning -- saying that your client had been prejudiced by this delay in the issuance of the subpoena. Are you ready to go forward without the documents that you have requested?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. We will start trial next Monday if the Trial Chamber will order it tomorrow, or two weeks, or one week, or ten days. We want to proceed. We have been asking to proceed since last Fall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Then as far as your subpoena request, that will not play a role in your readiness for trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine. We will see if we can resolve that. I think Mr Rivkin makes the point, though, when he says that this issue goes -- of course -- the primary issue is General Blaskic, because he is the one who is in custody. He has been in custody 12 months, however, and it seems to me that we should approach this issue very carefully, and I wonder whether if any action that we were to take in terms of additional briefing that might result in a month's extension in terms of briefing, that is time for Croatia and time for the Prosecution, whether that in the scheme of things, in the scheme of things really makes a difference, particularly when you have just -- perhaps will just issue a subpoena if it is signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This issue would disappear if the Prosecutor will represent that the pendency of this matter will not be raised at tomorrow's status conference or thereafter as a reason to delay the trial of General Blaskic. If they are in a position to make that representation, then I have no objection to whatever briefing schedule or further proceedings that the court would like to hold on the broader issue of subpoenas, etc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me tell you. We have to issue a Decision, and I can tell you that as much as I have read already, and I have read a lot, I think that all judges benefit from full briefing, and sometimes the time to issue a Decision is reduced by the amount of assistance that you have. Yes, we have had a lot of assistance and I have read every word, I suppose -- almost -- so I think it might be of some assistance to have the briefing, and it may cut the time down for the Decision. You still have to wait for our Decision. You realise that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For a trial, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I hope not. I would not expect so. The Prosecution did not seek their subpoena until more than a year after the indictment of the case. For them to now say, if they so argue tomorrow, that they cannot go to trial because they waited a year to seek a subpoena and then got embroiled in this dispute I think would be outlandish. I am simply asking if the Prosecutor is in a position to represent that they will not raise the pendency of this matter as a reason they cannot proceed to trial expeditiously, I have no objection to any briefing schedule that would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is exactly why I did not want to handle this matter. I wanted it to be handled all by the other Trial Chamber. Somehow I draw the black bean always. I do not know what to do. JUSTICE ARBOUR: I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I do not really want to put you on the spot at this point, because I do not know what you are going to say. JUSTICE ARBOUR: I may be of assistance. I certainly cannot undertake that we would not make representation that we need the time. As it turns out, we go first and we carry a burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Obviously we are serious about getting these documents. Meanwhile I would be certainly very happy to continue pending the decision and whatever reasonable time is allocated for briefings to continue with the Republic of Croatia under the umbrella of the previous arrangement to examine whether compliance can be achieved. I certainly would not want that process to be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Hayman, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You may have two weeks to submit additional briefing, Mr Rivkin. Keep in mind that we are more interested in substance than form. So typos, beautiful language is not necessarily important. If you have authorities that you wish us to look at, you must attach those, because we have limited access to authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Sure, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Two weeks to submit the brief. If you are able to submit it to the Prosecution in ten days, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: We will undertake to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution will then have ten days after receipt of the first draft, if you receive a first draft, of the brief to submit your reply. Now, as to the trial date, I am not involved in that, but I will volunteer my services to sit with the Prosecution and the lawyer who represents Croatia to see if we can resolve -- if you wish me to -- believe me, I have no desire -- if you wish me to resolve the request that you have made, because I have suspended the subpoena, and I understand you are trying to work together. If you want me to be present, I will be present. If not, that is fine with me too. Mr Hayman, I understand that you would object at this time, but what I am telling you once again is giving two weeks and then ten days, that is a month basically, does not mean that our decision would be issued a month earlier than if we had to wait for the briefing. I would hope that with good briefing we are able to expedite the issuance of a Decision. So we may get to that point. Whether it is going to delay your trial, that is something you will have to deal with with Judge Jorda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a different comment to make, your Honour. I was not going to comment on the schedule. May I make that comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is, given the willingness of Bosnia-Herzegovina to accept the process, I would ask whatever process is set up to facilitate production of documents to the Prosecution, the same process, a parallel process, should be set up on the same schedule as to the Defence's request to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I will be happy to resolve that as well. That is, if you are having problems obtaining documents from Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would be very happy to sit with you or to do whatever is necessary to help you in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are obtaining no documents from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: When you file your subpoena. Maybe you are not following me or I am not following you. I do not want to be involved in this. The only reason is that the subpoena has been suspended as to Croatia. They are now attempting to provide documents on a voluntary basis. If I can facilitate that, I am happy to. I do not know that I need to be involved in your situation yet, because you have not filed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Should I infer from that that our subpoena will issue prior to any ruling on the broader issue by this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It will not not issue because of the legal issue pending. Still Judge Jan will have to make a determination after talking with you and looking ex parte with you, discussing the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is a Decision he has to make. The pendency of the issue of whether this Tribunal has the power to issue a subpoena will not affect it in any way, because, as you rightly point out, Bosnia-Herzegovina does not object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you do not have the power, the mere fact they do not object will not make the subpoena legal, if you do not have the power. Plainly because the government says they have no objection, how will that make it legal? Examine this question when you come before me tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We will, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me. May I ask you to clarify if we are talking about 14 days or 14 working days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: 14 working days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: 14 working days from today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: 14 working days from today. Ten working days from the date that you receive their draft, if it is a draft that is of some substance. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Prosecutor? JUSTICE ARBOUR: I take it that the draft that triggers our obligation to reply is the final product except for form; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It has to be one of substance. If you get it and you consider it is not appropriate to trigger a response, then you need to contact me. We will have a representative from Croatia present, we will take a look at it and see whether or not this is something you can respond to. Is there anything further now from the Prosecution? JUSTICE ARBOUR: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr Hayman? Madame Vidovic? MME VIDOVIC: Your Honour, I will be very brief. So far the Defence of General Blaskic -- and when I say us, I mean Bosnia-Herzegovina -- has still not turned to us for production of any evidence. Had they addressed us, we would have provided the evidence that they asked. I think that we have been cooperative as far as production of evidence is concerned in every case so far, even those that could be seen as exculpatory to General Blaskic. So we have not been asked to produce any evidence, and my understanding is that an order to produce evidence is only issued when a state is not producing it. That is not showing willingness to do so. I would very much like to see what evidence the counsel has in mind and we will not oppose it. All I am trying to say is that in this case, as in all other cases, they can all be resolved in this manner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps you should make yourself available tomorrow to meet with -- it will be up to Judge Jan -- and maybe even with Mr Hayman to see what can be done. Now that is a very issue that Croatia has raised. Do not send a subpoena until you ask for the documents first. We are trying to stay out of that issue if we can. In light of your prior association with the Tribunal, and I have seen you dozens -- not dozens -- perhaps a dozen times here in proceedings and in exchanges that we have at the Tribunal, perhaps there is a way, if you meet with Mr Hayman, to expedite the production of some of those documents, but -- excuse me a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Hayman? Do you want to say something? I am prepared to look at your list and give you the documents on their own. You do not need a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The government has our applications, I presume. They were served on them, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is not so, she is saying. Why do you not meet her first before you see me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not think so, your Honour. On the eve of trial? We are happy to try to get the documents cooperatively, but to protect our client's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why go through this process?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To protect our client's interests, your Honour, we would pursue a form of compulsion to obtain the documents. Whatever the most compulsive process is that the Tribunal is empowered to use, we need to have it in place going forward to protect our client's interests, given the eve of trial. If it turns out that it is unnecessary in the sense that we do not come to that later bridge, that is great. We will be thrilled, but I think absolutely it is required to protect my client's interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A list will go to them in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It will go to them right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They will give you these documents. Why go through this process of getting a subpoena issued? They will come to know the documents you want in any case. Why do you want to use the compulsory force of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My obligation to my client --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you just one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Miss Vidovic, have you seen the subpoena that Mr Hayman wishes to have issued? MME VIDOVIC: I saw it very briefly, very briefly indeed. I was actually told by the Prosecutor's office that it has been served on Bosnia-Herzegovina. I only had a cursory look at it, so I really do not know in detail what is contained in it, but I believe that Bosnia-Herzegovina would produce all the evidence in its possession, because so far we have produced all evidence both inculpatory and exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You understand Mr Hayman's position and that is he needs some kind of a court document because he is facing a potential trial date? It may serve you well to provide a copy of the subpoena as soon as we conclude our proceedings on Miss Vidovic, let Miss Vidovic look at it tonight. Tomorrow you are to meet with Judge Jan at 10.15. Is that the time you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I believe, Miss Vidovic, if you are available tomorrow -- are you available in the morning -- can you make yourself available in the morning? MME VIDOVIC: Yes. I could be here. However, it is a different matter at issue. I need to consult with the proper authorities so that we can determine what documents are in our possession and what are not. In other words, I have to consult with the proper authorities to determine the whereabouts of the documents, and I think that that is a way to accelerate the process, and I think that it may take a shorter period of time than it would take by issuing a subpoena. I think that the position of -- I understand the position of the accused and of his counsel, but I would like for an equal balancing handling of the situation so that the interests of the victims are protected as well as the defence of the accused, and this is why I am making this comment. However, we will certainly turn over all documents and produce all the documents required regardless of the decision of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think perhaps the two of you need to talk at the end of our proceedings and see what can be done, and, of course, I understand your position that it is the -- you want some official request that would perhaps trigger the time running, and in case there are some things that occur over which you have no control, at least you have your piece of paper signed by a judge saying: "Do it."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAJ
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam. Just to put the record straight, I think when we had the last hearing on subpoena I pointed out that there was no previous communications to the Government of Croatia before the subpoena to Croatia was issued, just so that we have it in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I recall that, but now, since we three judges are in the midst of this, perhaps we can encourage a different approach, not that it is required, and we are not saying that it is required, but we are just trying to reach a result the best way we can. So do you understand -- I understand your position and I think it is well taken, but perhaps if you talk with Miss Vidovic, perhaps you will be able to get some feel about how documents are maintained, even what documents may exist, that kind of thing. It is a better way to ask for documents, all of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am eager to speak with her, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Those terrible things that you have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I join in your comments, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Good. Are there any other matters that anyone else wishes to say? Thank you very much. On behalf of the Trial Chamber we want to thank the lawyers in attendance and the amici.
